dialogue.scene: Ms Huda explains a science project to her class. Reem checks the details.

p1.t: For this project, you'll work in pairs and make a poster about saving water.
Sorry, Ms Huda, can I just get this straight? We choose our own partner, don't we?
Yes, you do. Each poster also needs a short report with a word limit of two hundred words.
Do you mean a written report, not a spoken one?
Yes, a written one, please.

p2.t: The due date is the fifteenth of March.
So you're saying we hand in the poster and the report together?
Exactly. Bring both to class on that day.
Could you clarify one more thing? We can use photos from the internet, can't we?
Yes, but you must write where each photo comes from.

dialogue.focus: So you're saying we hand in the poster and the report together?

p2.t: Oh, there's a change of plan. Khalid can't come until five.
So you're saying we should meet at five instead?
Yes. My dad can pick you up at half past four.

p1.t: Good morning. Could I speak to Mrs Al-Harbi, please?
I'm sorry, she's out at the moment. Can I take a message?
Yes, please. It's about the sofa she ordered. We can deliver it on Tuesday between ten and twelve.
Sorry, it's a bad line. Did you say Tuesday or Thursday?
Tuesday, the day after Monday.

p2.t: Please ask her to call me back. My name is Yazeed.
Hold on, let me get a pen. Could you spell your name, please?
Y-A-Z-E-E-D. And could she confirm her address, too?

dialogue.scene: Reem is helping her grandmother make kleija, a date biscuit from the Qassim region.

p1.t: What are we making today, Grandma? It's kleija, isn't it?
Yes! First, preheat the oven to one hundred and eighty degrees.
Done. And then we mix flour, butter and two tablespoons of sugar?
That's right. Then stir in a pinch of cardamom. Just a pinch, because it's very strong.
Mmm, it smells lovely already.

p2.t: What's next? Could you clarify how we add the dates?
First, roll out the dough. Then spread the date paste on top.
So you're saying we put the dates on the flat dough and then roll it up like a carpet?
Exactly, and then we cut it into small pieces. It'll make sense when you see it.
Let's try it! I'll wash my hands.

dialogue.focus: So you're saying we put the dates on the flat dough and then roll it up like a carpet?

expressions.frame: The most thoughtful gift I've received was ___.

expressions.def: worth the price you pay
expressions.frame: ___ is good value for money.

expressions.def: finally, after thinking about it
expressions.frame: In the end, we decided to ___.

dialogue.scene: Reem and her brother Omar want to buy a present for their mother's birthday.

p1.t: Mum's birthday is next week. Have you come up with any ideas for a present?
What about a new handbag? She'd love one.
She would, but a good handbag is really expensive. I can't afford one.
We could split the cost. Or perfume? It isn't as expensive, but it's not very personal.
True. Let's keep thinking.

p2.t: What about a photo book with pictures of the family? It's much cheaper than a handbag, and it's more thoughtful.
I love that idea! It's good value for money, too.
So it would be better to make a photo book than to buy a bag?
Definitely. Let's go for the photo book. Mum will cry happy tears!
In the end, the best gifts come from the heart.

dialogue.focus: Let's go for the photo book.
qs: Why don't they buy a handbag?
Why is the photo book a better gift?

speakout.scene: Your best friend's birthday is next week. You and another friend want to buy a gift together. I am your other friend. Compare ideas and decide.

prompts.q: I think we should buy a football shirt. What do you think?
prompts.hint: Compare it with another idea, using 'isn't as … as' or 'much more … than'.

prompts.q: But we only have one hundred riyals.
prompts.hint: Talk about money: 'We can't afford …' or 'We could split the cost.'

prompts.q: So, what's our final decision?
prompts.hint: Decide with 'Let's go for …' and say why it's good value for money or thoughtful.

culture.title: Gift-Giving Traditions
points: In Saudi Arabia, people often give perfume, oud or sweets as gifts.
In Japan, the way a gift is wrapped is almost as important as the gift itself.
In some countries, people open gifts later, not in front of the person who gave them.
qs: Do you prefer giving or receiving gifts? Why?
Is an expensive gift always better than a cheap one?

3-1.exit: Compare two gift ideas for someone in your family and say which one you'd go for and why.

3-2.objective: Today you will compare school clubs and choose the one that suits you.
3-2.warmup: Which after-school clubs or activities have you tried?

expressions.def: to like something a lot
expressions.frame: I'm really into ___ at the moment.

expressions.def: to think carefully about the good and bad points
expressions.frame: I need to weigh up ___ and ___ before I decide.

expressions.def: the good and bad points of something
expressions.frame: One of the pros of ___ is ___.

expressions.def: to be right for someone
expressions.frame: The ___ club would suit me because ___.

expressions.def: to start a new hobby or activity
expressions.frame: This year I'd like to take up ___.

expressions.def: to continue doing something
expressions.frame: I'm going to stick with ___ because ___.

dialogue.scene: Emma's school has three new clubs: robotics, drama and photography. Emma talks to her friend Noura.

p1.t: Have you made up your mind about the clubs yet?
Not yet. I'm weighing up the pros and cons. I'm really into robotics, but it's on Thursdays.
What's wrong with Thursdays?
I have swimming then. Drama is on Mondays, and it's just as fun as robotics.
I'm sure you'll find the right one.

p2.t: What about photography? You love taking pictures.
True, but I think drama would suit me better. I want to be more confident when I speak.
And you're already good at photography. Why not take up something new?
Exactly! So I'll go for drama and stick with swimming on Thursdays.
Great choice. Maybe I'll join drama too!

dialogue.focus: I think drama would suit me better.
qs: Why can't Emma join the robotics club?
Why does Emma choose drama?

speakout.scene: Your school offers three new clubs: chess, cooking and coding. You can join only one. I am your teacher. Tell me about your choice.

prompts.q: Which clubs are you interested in?
prompts.hint: Say what you're into and compare two clubs with 'just as … as' or 'not as … as'.

prompts.q: What are the pros and cons of each one?
prompts.hint: Give one pro and one con, using 'On the other hand, …'

prompts.q: So, have you made up your mind?
prompts.hint: Decide with 'I'll go for …' or '… would suit me better' and give a reason.

culture.title: After-School Activities
points: In Saudi Arabia, more and more schools offer clubs like robotics, art and sports.
In the USA, many students join clubs or teams after school, from chess to music.
Experts say clubs help students make friends and learn skills they can't learn in class.
qs: Which new club would you like your school to start?
Do you think after-school clubs are as important as lessons? Why?

3-2.exit: Tell me about two clubs or activities, compare them, and say which one would suit you better.

3-3.objective: Today you will compare holiday places and agree on where to go.
3-3.warmup: Where would you like to go on your next family holiday?

expressions.def: to go on holiday to have a break from normal life
expressions.frame: I'd love to get away to ___ for a few days.

expressions.def: to visit the famous places as a tourist
expressions.frame: In ___, I'd like to see the sights, like ___.

expressions.def: very far from towns and people
expressions.frame: I'd like to stay in a camp in the middle of nowhere because ___.

expressions.def: the answer changes because of something
expressions.frame: Where we go depends on ___.

expressions.def: the amount of money you can spend
expressions.frame: Our budget for the trip is ___.

expressions.def: to say something that is true or sensible
expressions.frame: You have a point. ___ is better because ___.

dialogue.scene: Faisal's family are choosing between Jeddah and AlUla for the mid-year holiday.

p1.t: We need to get away for a few days. Should we go to Jeddah or AlUla?
Jeddah! We can swim in the Red Sea and see the sights in Al-Balad.
That's true. But AlUla isn't nearly as busy as Jeddah, and the rocks are amazing.
Yes, but AlUla is in the middle of nowhere. There's not much to do in the evening.
Ha! There's more than you think.

p2.t: It depends on our budget, too. The hotels in AlUla are expensive, but maybe it's worth it.
You have a point. So it would be better to go to Jeddah this time, wouldn't it?
I think so. And we can visit AlUla in spring, when it isn't as cold at night.
Perfect. Let's go for Jeddah! I'll pack my swimming goggles.
Great. Then it's decided.

dialogue.focus: So it would be better to go to Jeddah this time, wouldn't it?
qs: Why does Dad like AlUla?
Why does the family decide to go to Jeddah?

speakout.scene: Your family has a long weekend. You can go to Abha, the Red Sea coast or a desert camp. I am your parent. Help us make up our minds.

prompts.q: So, where should we go this time?
prompts.hint: Compare two places with 'isn't as … as' or 'much more … than'.

prompts.q: But our budget isn't very big.
prompts.hint: Answer with 'It depends on …' or 'You have a point, but …'

prompts.q: OK, what's your final choice?
prompts.hint: Decide with 'It would be better to go to …' or 'Let's go for …' and give a reason.

culture.title: Holidays by the Red Sea
points: The Red Sea coast has some of the most beautiful coral reefs in the world.
Saudi Arabia is building new eco-friendly resorts on islands in the Red Sea.
Al-Balad, the old part of Jeddah, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site with old coral houses.
qs: Would you rather visit a beach or a historical place? Why?
Why do you think eco-friendly hotels are important?

3-3.exit: Compare two holiday places in Saudi Arabia and tell me which one you'd go for and why.

3-4.objective: Today you will compare food options and decide what to order.
3-4.warmup: What's your favourite restaurant? What do you usually order?

expressions.def: to want to have or do something
expressions.frame: I really fancy some ___ tonight.

expressions.def: to find it hard to choose one of two things
expressions.frame: I can't decide between ___ and ___.

expressions.def: both choices are OK for me
expressions.frame: Pizza or ___? Either is fine with me.

expressions.def: making your stomach feel full
expressions.frame: ___ is very filling, so I can't eat much of it.

expressions.def: to not eat or use too much of something
expressions.frame: I'm trying to go easy on ___.

expressions.def: shared by two or more people
expressions.frame: Let's get one ___ between us.

dialogue.scene: Omar and his sister Reem are at a food court with their uncle, choosing dinner.

p1.t: So, what do you fancy tonight? Burgers, shawarma or Japanese?
I can't decide between burgers and shawarma. Either is fine with me.
Well, a burger meal is very filling, and it isn't as healthy as the shawarma plate with salad.
That's true. And I had burgers yesterday, so I should go easy on fast food.
Good thinking, Omar.

p2.t: What about you, Reem? It's up to you.
Hmm, sushi looks good, but it's more expensive than the other places.
Don't worry about the price today. You choose.
Then it would be better to get one big plate between us. It's cheaper than two small ones.
Great idea. Let's go for the big sushi plate, and the shawarma for Omar!

dialogue.focus: Then it would be better to get one big plate between us.
qs: Why does Omar decide not to have a burger?
Why does Reem want one big sushi plate?

speakout.scene: You and your friend are at a restaurant with a small budget. The menu has pizza, grills and salads. I am your friend. Decide what to order together.

prompts.q: Everything looks good! What do you fancy?
prompts.hint: Say what you can't decide between, and compare them with 'isn't as … as'.

prompts.q: Pizza is very filling, though.
prompts.hint: Agree or disagree, and suggest something with 'It would be better to …'

prompts.q: OK, so what shall we order?
prompts.hint: Make the final decision with 'Let's go for …' or 'Let's get one … between us.'

culture.title: Eating Out in Saudi Arabia
points: Eating out with family and friends is a popular activity in Saudi Arabia, especially at night.
Food trucks selling coffee, burgers and desserts are now common in many Saudi cities.
Saudi restaurants show calories on their menus to help people choose healthier food.
qs: Do you look at the calories on menus? Why or why not?
Is home-made food better than restaurant food? Why?

3-4.exit: Tell me about two dishes you can't decide between, compare them, and make your choice.

3-5.objective: Today you will discuss options with a group and reach a final decision.
3-5.warmup: Have you ever had to make a decision with a group? How did you decide?

expressions.def: to finally decide after discussing
expressions.frame: After a long talk, we reached a decision to ___.

expressions.def: the best choice
expressions.frame: I think the best option is ___ because ___.

expressions.def: to collect money for a good reason
expressions.frame: We could raise money for ___ by ___.

expressions.def: to have a good effect on people or things
expressions.frame: I want to make a difference by ___.

expressions.def: to decide by counting what most people want
expressions.frame: Let's take a vote on ___.

expressions.def: to agree with an idea or decision
expressions.frame: I'll go along with ___ because ___.

dialogue.scene: Sam, Fahad and Khalid must choose a class project: a bake sale for charity, a school garden or a beach clean-up.

p1.t: OK, we need to reach a decision today. Bake sale, garden or beach clean-up?
I think a bake sale is the best option. We could raise money for the children's hospital.
Good idea, but a garden would last much longer. It isn't as quick as a bake sale, though.
Let's weigh up the pros and cons. A beach clean-up would make a difference, but the beach is far away.
That's true. Transport would be a problem.

p2.t: So it's between the bake sale and the garden. Why don't we take a vote?
Good idea. I vote for the garden. It would be better to make something the whole school can enjoy.
Hmm, I still prefer the bake sale, but I'll go along with the group.
Then let's go for the garden! Maybe we can do a bake sale next term to buy the plants.
Perfect. That's a decision everyone can be happy with.

dialogue.focus: Then let's go for the garden!
qs: Why doesn't the group choose the beach clean-up?
How do they finally reach a decision?

speakout.scene: Your class has 2,000 riyals to improve the school. The options are new sports equipment, a reading corner or a water fountain. Discuss them with me and reach a decision.

prompts.q: So, which option do you think is best?
prompts.hint: Choose one and compare it with another, using 'not as … as' or 'much more … than'.

prompts.q: But a reading corner would be useful for everyone.
prompts.hint: Weigh up the pros and cons: give one good and one bad point, using 'On the other hand'.

prompts.q: We need to decide now. What's your final answer?
prompts.hint: Reach a decision with 'Let's go for …' or 'It would be better to …', or say you'll go along with my idea.

culture.title: Young People Making a Difference
points: In Saudi Arabia, many young people volunteer at big events, for example during Ramadan or Riyadh Season.
Saudi Vision 2030 aims to have one million volunteers every year.
Around the world, students organise beach clean-ups, bake sales and tree-planting days.
qs: What problem in your neighbourhood would you like to solve?
Is it better to give money or to give your time? Why?

3-5.exit: Tell me about two project ideas, compare them, and say what decision you would reach and why.

words.ex: Please hand in your essays on Sunday.
The due date is next Thursday, isn't it?
Today we're going to work in pairs.
Let me get this straight: the test is on Monday?
Could you clarify the last question, please?
The word limit for the story is 150 words.

dialogue.t: For this project, you'll work in pairs and make a poster about saving water.
Sorry, Ms Huda, can I just get this straight? We choose our own partner, don't we?
Yes, you do. Each poster also needs a short report with a word limit of two hundred words.
Do you mean a written report, not a spoken one?
Yes, a written one, please.
The due date is the fifteenth of March.
So you're saying we hand in the poster and the report together?
Exactly. Bring both to class on that day.

grammar.title: Question tags with be and do
grammar.ar: ذيل السؤال: نضيف سؤالاً قصيراً في آخر الجملة للتأكد من المعلومة. إذا كانت الجملة مثبتة يكون الذيل منفياً، وإذا كانت منفية يكون مثبتاً.
examples: The due date is Thursday, isn't it?
We choose our own partners, don't we?
It isn't a group project, is it?

words.ex: We usually meet up at the park on Fridays.
My mum will pick me up at five.
Please be on time for the game.
Can you confirm the time tonight?
There's a change of plan. We're meeting at six.
A picnic on Friday? Count me in!

dialogue.t: Are you free on Friday? A few of us want to meet up at the trampoline park.
Count me in! It's the new one near the mall, isn't it?
That's right. We're meeting there at four o'clock.
Let me get this straight: four in the afternoon, not four in the morning?
Oh, there's a change of plan. Khalid can't come until five.
So you're saying we should meet at five instead?
Yes. My dad can pick you up at half past four.
Great. Could you send me a message later to confirm the time?

grammar.title: Question tags with the present continuous and can
grammar.ar: إذا كان في الجملة فعل مساعد مثل is / are / can نكرّره في الذيل: We're meeting at four, aren't we?
examples: We're meeting at four, aren't we?
Your dad can pick us up, can't he?
Khalid isn't coming, is he?

words.ex: Dad is busy. Can I take a message?
Hold on, I'll get my mum.
I'll call you back in ten minutes.
It's a bad line. I can't hear you.
Could you spell your family name, please?
I'll pass on the message to my brother.

dialogue.t: Good morning. Could I speak to Mrs Al-Harbi, please?
I'm sorry, she's out at the moment. Can I take a message?
Yes, please. It's about the sofa she ordered. We can deliver it on Tuesday between ten and twelve.
Sorry, it's a bad line. Did you say Tuesday or Thursday?
Please ask her to call me back. My name is Yazeed.
Hold on, let me get a pen. Could you spell your name, please?
Y-A-Z-E-E-D. And could she confirm her address, too?
So you're saying the sofa arrives on Tuesday morning and she should call you back?

grammar.title: Checking questions: Did you say …? / So you're saying …
grammar.ar: نستخدم Did you say …? لنسأل عن كلمة لم نسمعها جيداً، ونستخدم So you're saying … لنعيد المعلومة بكلماتنا ونتأكد منها.
examples: Sorry, did you say Tuesday or Thursday?
So you're saying she should call you back?
Could you spell that, please?

words.ex: Don't worry if you get lost. Just ask someone.
Go past the bank and turn left.
The pharmacy is on your left.
Take the escalator up to the food court.
Kingdom Centre is a famous landmark in Riyadh.
It's a huge red building. You can't miss it!

dialogue.t: Excuse me, I think I've got lost. How do I get to the cinema?
No problem. Go past the fountain and turn right at the bookshop.
Go past the fountain, then turn right at the bookshop. Is that right?
Yes. Then take the escalator up to the second floor.
Sorry, one more question. The cinema is right next to the escalator, isn't it?
Not quite. When you get off the escalator, it's on your left, next to the food court.
Let me get this straight. Do you mean the food court with the big clock?
Exactly. The clock is a good landmark. You can't miss it!

grammar.title: Checking directions
grammar.ar: عندما يعطيك أحد الاتجاهات، كرّر ما سمعته ثم اسأل Is that right? أو استخدم Do you mean …? للتأكد من المكان.
examples: Turn left at the bookshop. Is that right?
Do you mean the bookshop next to the bank?
It's on the second floor, isn't it?

words.ex: Preheat the oven to 180 degrees.
Add two tablespoons of honey.
Add a pinch of salt to the soup.
Stir in the milk slowly.
Roll out the dough on the table.
Now the recipe makes sense to me.

dialogue.t: What are we making today, Grandma? It's kleija, isn't it?
Yes! First, preheat the oven to one hundred and eighty degrees.
Done. And then we mix flour, butter and two tablespoons of sugar?
That's right. Then stir in a pinch of cardamom. Just a pinch, because it's very strong.
What's next? Could you clarify how we add the dates?
First, roll out the dough. Then spread the date paste on top.
So you're saying we put the dates on the flat dough and then roll it up like a carpet?
Exactly, and then we cut it into small pieces. It'll make sense when you see it.

grammar.title: Question tags with the present simple
grammar.ar: مع المضارع البسيط نستخدم do / does / don't / doesn't في الذيل: We add sugar, don't we? / It comes from Qassim, doesn't it?
examples: We add sugar, don't we?
Kleija comes from Qassim, doesn't it?
We don't need eggs, do we?

words.ex: We set off early to avoid the traffic.
It's getting dark. Let's head back.
Don't forget your permission slip!
I made a packed lunch for the trip.
Make sure you bring a hat.
Just to double-check, the bus leaves at six, doesn't it?

dialogue.t: Great news! Next month our class is going on a two-day trip to AlUla.
Amazing! Just to double-check, we'll stay there for one night, won't we?
Yes. We'll set off from school at six on Wednesday morning and head back on Thursday evening.
Six in the morning! I'll need to go to bed early.
Please hand in your permission slips by Sunday, and make sure you bring a packed lunch for the bus.
Let me get this straight. Do you mean a packed lunch for the first day only?
Exactly. All the other meals are included in the price.
So you're saying we only need pocket money for souvenirs. Great!

grammar.title: Question tags with will and the past simple
grammar.ar: مع will يكون الذيل won't، ومع الماضي البسيط نستخدم didn't / did: We'll stay one night, won't we? / You said six, didn't you?
examples: We'll stay one night, won't we?
You said six o'clock, didn't you?
We won't need much money, will we?

words.ex: There was an announcement about the school trip.
I need to catch up on my homework.
I was away. Can you fill me in?
The final will take place on Friday.
According to Ms Huda, the test is easy.
I signed up for the chess club.

dialogue.t: I missed school yesterday. Can you fill me in? Was there any news?
Yes, there was a big announcement. Mr Khalid said that sports day would take place next Thursday.
Next Thursday? That's soon! Did he say anything about the races?
He told us that everyone had to sign up for at least one race.
What else did I miss? I need to catch up on everything.
Ms Huda said that our science test would be on Monday.
Oh no! Did she say which pages we need to study?
According to Ms Huda, it's pages twenty to thirty-five. She told us to bring a calculator, too.

grammar.title: Reported statements: say and tell
grammar.ar: نستخدم said بدون ذكر الشخص: He said that…، ونستخدم told مع الشخص: He told us that…. ويرجع الزمن خطوة إلى الماضي: is → was، will → would.
examples: 'Sports day is on Thursday.' → He said that sports day was on Thursday.
'The test will be on Monday.' → She told us that the test would be on Monday.
'Bring a calculator.' → She told us to bring a calculator.

words.ex: I keep in touch with my cousins online.
Guess what? We're going to Abha!
My friend moved house last summer.
There's a new arrival in our family.
We get together at Grandpa's every Friday.
Grandma sends her love to you.

dialogue.t: Was that Aunt Maha? Fill me in! What did she say?
Guess what? She said that her family was moving house next month.
Really? Where are they going?
She told me they had bought a flat near the sea in Khobar.
Did she say anything about Cousin Lulwa?
Yes! She said there was a new arrival in the family. Lulwa had a baby brother called Hamad.
That's wonderful! Are we going to visit them?
She said we would all get together at Eid. And she sends her love to you.

grammar.title: Changing tenses in reported speech
grammar.ar: عند نقل الكلام: المضارع يصبح ماضياً (are moving → were moving)، والمضارع التام أو الماضي يصبح ماضياً تاماً (have bought → had bought)، وwill تصبح would.
examples: 'We are moving house.' → She said they were moving house.
'We have bought a flat.' → She told me they had bought a flat.
'We will visit at Eid.' → She said they would visit at Eid.

words.ex: He scored a goal in the last minute.
I'm proud of my little sister.
Don't give up. You can do it!
The coach spoke at the press conference.
He admitted that he was nervous.
Everyone cheered at the final whistle.

dialogue.t: Did you watch the match last night? Saudi Arabia beat Japan two-one!
Yes! I watched the press conference afterwards, too.
What did the captain say?
He said that he was proud of the team because they hadn't given up.
And what about the player who scored the winning goal?
He told reporters that it was the best moment of his life. He said he would never forget it.
What did the coach say?
He admitted that the team had played badly in the first half, but he said they would get better.

grammar.title: Reporting verbs: say, tell, admit
grammar.ar: نستخدم أفعالاً لنقل الكلام: said (قال)، told + شخص (أخبر)، admitted (اعترف)، وبعدها that مع تغيير الزمن.
examples: 'I'm proud of the team.' → He said he was proud of the team.
'We played badly.' → He admitted that they had played badly.
'I'll never forget it.' → He told reporters he would never forget it.

words.ex: Let me show you around the school.
He wanted to know my name.
I wonder if it will rain tomorrow.
She settled in quickly at her new school.
I get on well with my classmates.
I made friends with a boy from Egypt.

dialogue.t: How was school? I heard there's a new student in your class.
Yes, his name's Youssef. He's from Cairo. The teacher asked me to show him around.
That's kind of you. What did he want to know?
He asked me where the library was, and he asked if we had a football team.
Is he settling in well? I wonder if he misses Cairo.
I think he's fine. He asked me whether the teachers were strict.
And what did you say?
I told him they were strict but kind. He also wanted to know what time school finished.

grammar.title: Reported questions
grammar.ar: في السؤال المنقول نستخدم asked + if/whether لأسئلة نعم/لا، وasked + كلمة السؤال (where/what). ونرتّب الجملة مثل الجملة العادية بدون do/does وبدون علامة استفهام.
examples: 'Do you have a football team?' → He asked if we had a football team.
'Where is the library?' → He asked me where the library was.
'What time does school finish?' → He wanted to know what time school finished.

words.ex: Heavy rain is expected tomorrow.
We stayed indoors because of the storm.
They warned us about the strong wind.
The headline said 'Big Win for Saudi Team!'
I came across an old photo of my dad.
The team made an amazing discovery.

dialogue.t: You look excited. What's happening?
I saw the weather report. The reporter said there would be heavy rain in Riyadh tomorrow.
Really? Rain in Riyadh? Did they say anything else?
They warned people to stay indoors if possible, and they said schools might close.
What was the other story?
I came across an amazing headline online. According to the article, Saudi scientists have made a discovery in the Red Sea.
What kind of discovery?
The scientists said that they had found a new type of coral. They told reporters it could live in very warm water.

grammar.title: Reporting commands and warnings
grammar.ar: لنقل الأوامر والتحذيرات: told / warned + شخص + to + الفعل، وفي النفي not to + الفعل. وتصبح may → might و can → could.
examples: 'Stay indoors.' → They warned people to stay indoors.
'Don't drive in the rain.' → They told people not to drive in the rain.
'Schools may close.' → The reporter said schools might close.

words.ex: We interviewed the head teacher.
I always take notes in science lessons.
Let's find out who planted the trees.
We need a good quote for the report.
Breaking news: our team won the cup!
We go live on the school radio at seven.

dialogue.t: We go live on the school radio tomorrow. Did you interview the head teacher?
Yes, and I took notes. He said that the new garden would open next week.
Great! Did you find out who planted the trees?
He told me that students from every class had helped. He also asked if we could write a poem for the opening.
I interviewed Uncle Salem, the gardener. I asked him what his favourite plant was.
What did he say? We need a good quote.
He said, "Every plant needs love and water." Then he told me to remind everyone not to walk on the grass.
According to him, the grass is still very young. OK, let's start the report with "Breaking news"!

grammar.title: Statements, questions and commands together
grammar.ar: في التقرير الإخباري نجمع: said that للجمل، وasked if/what للأسئلة، وtold … (not) to للأوامر.
examples: He said that the garden would open next week.

pages.text: Sara was helping her grandmother clean the storeroom of their old family house in Jeddah when she found a dusty leather box. Inside was a heavy silver camera with a small clock carved on its side. "That belonged to my father," Grandma Huda said quietly. "Be careful with it. He used to say it could remember things that people forget."

Later, alone on the roof, Sara lifted the camera and pointed it at the carved wooden window across the street. When she pressed the button, there was a bright flash, and the ground seemed to disappear under her feet. The noise of the cars faded, and she heard street sellers and bicycle bells instead. She opened her eyes and gasped: the building looked brand new, and the street was full of people in old-fashioned clothes.

A calendar in a shop window said 1965. Sara's heart was beating fast, but she tried to stay calm and think. Near a fountain, a girl about her age was searching the ground, and her eyes were red from crying. "It's my father's ring," the girl said when Sara asked. "I promised to take it to the jeweller for him, and now it's gone."

Sara offered to help, and the two girls walked back along every street the girl had passed through. The girl's name was Huda, and she had the same dimple in her cheek as Sara's grandmother. "What a strange yellow watch!" Huda said, looking at Sara's wrist. Sara suddenly felt dizzy. She was standing next to her own grandmother as a twelve-year-old girl!

They looked under market tables, behind sacks of spices and between the stones of the old road, but they found nothing. Then Sara remembered a story Grandma Huda had told her many times: "A strange girl once helped me find my father's ring. She found it in the one place I never thought to look." Sara noticed a small hole in the side of Huda's cloth bag. "Have you checked inside the lining of your bag?" she asked.

Huda pushed her fingers through the torn lining, and her face lit up. The gold ring had been hiding there all along! She hugged Sara tightly and asked, "Who are you? Will I ever see you again?" Sara smiled and answered, "I'm sure you will, but you might have to wait a long time."

Sara walked to a quiet corner and turned the camera towards herself. She wasn't sure it would work, but she took a deep breath and pressed the button. Once again there was a flash, and the sounds of the old market faded away. When she opened her eyes, she was back on the roof, and the evening call to prayer was echoing across the modern city.

Downstairs, Grandma Huda was sitting in her usual chair, holding a cup of tea. She looked carefully at Sara's yellow watch and smiled, as if she had been waiting for this moment for years. "I've waited sixty years to say thank you," she said softly, and she held up her hand. On her finger shone a familiar gold ring.

options: She wanted to buy the same watch
She thought the watch was broken
She realised Sara was the girl who helped her long ago

stories.title: The Night the Lights Went Out

pages.text: Every summer, Faisal and his younger sister Noura stayed with their grandfather on the Farasan Islands. Grandfather Saleh had been a fisherman for forty years, and he knew every beach by name. "The turtles will come soon," he told them one evening. "They have returned to this sand for thousands of years."

That week, something new had appeared near the beach: a bright café with colourful lights. Every night, the lights shone across the water until midnight. Noura thought the café looked beautiful, but Grandfather frowned when he saw it. "Baby turtles find the sea by following the light of the moon on the water," he explained quietly. "Those lights could cause a big problem."

Ten days later, Faisal woke up after midnight and couldn't get back to sleep. He walked to the window and noticed small dark shapes moving across the sand. At first, he thought they were crabs. Then his heart jumped, because they were baby turtles, hundreds of them, and they were heading away from the sea, towards the café and the busy road behind it!

Faisal woke Noura and Grandfather, and they ran outside with a bucket and a torch. "Don't use the torch!" Grandfather warned. "It will confuse them even more." They gently picked up the tiny hatchlings one by one and carried them back to the water's edge. But more and more were climbing out of the nest, and the café lights were still burning brightly.

"We have to turn off those lights," Faisal said, breathing hard. He raced to the café, where a young man named Majed was cleaning tables. At first, Majed looked annoyed. "Turn off my lights? Customers won't come if the place is dark," he said.

"Please, just come and see," Faisal begged. Majed followed him to the beach, and when he saw the little turtles crawling towards the road, his face changed. Without another word, he ran back and switched off every light. Slowly, the beach became dark and silent, and the moon shone silver on the waves. Almost at once, the baby turtles turned around and hurried towards the sea.

They worked until sunrise, checking the sand for any turtles that had got lost. By morning, they had rescued nearly two hundred hatchlings. Majed sat down on the sand, tired but smiling. "I had no idea," he said. "I'll find a better way to light my café."

A month later, the café opened again with soft orange lamps that faced away from the beach. Majed hung a sign on the door: "Turtle-Friendly Café: Lights Low from June to September." Many customers came to hear the story of the turtle rescue, and the café became more popular than ever. Grandfather smiled proudly at Faisal and Noura. "The sea has some new friends," he said.

options: By following the light of the moon on the water
By listening to the sound of the waves

options: Because the light would confuse the turtles more
Because it would wake the neighbours

options: Grandfather ordered him to do it
He saw the baby turtles going towards the road

options: Protecting nature can also be good for business
Majed was still angry with Faisal

pages.text: It was a hot afternoon in the mountains near Taif, and Hamad was walking along the edge of his grandfather's farm. Suddenly, he heard a strange, high cry coming from the old wire fence. He ran towards the sound and stopped in surprise. A young falcon was hanging upside down, and one of its wings was caught in the sharp wire.

The bird was frightened, and it was beating its free wing wildly. Hamad remembered something his grandfather had taught him: a falcon becomes calm when it cannot see. He took off his outer shirt and gently covered the bird's head. Then, slowly and carefully, he pulled the wire away from its feathers until the falcon was free.

Hamad carried the falcon home, holding it close to his chest. His grandfather looked at the wing and shook his head. "It isn't bleeding badly, but it's hurt," he said. "It needs a vet, and the falcon clinic is in the city." Just then, a large white car stopped outside their gate, and a man in sunglasses stepped out.

"That's a beautiful bird," the man said, smiling. "I'll give you five thousand riyals for it right now." Hamad's eyes went wide, because with that much money he could buy the new laptop he had wanted for a whole year. But then he noticed the small metal cage in the back of the man's car. "Thank you, but it isn't for sale," Hamad said politely. "It's injured, and it belongs in the sky, not in a cage."

After the man drove away, his grandfather put a hand on Hamad's shoulder. "I'm proud of you," he said quietly. That evening, Hamad's uncle drove them to the falcon clinic, where a kind vet examined the bird. "Good news," she said. "The wing isn't broken, but the falcon must rest for two weeks before it can fly again."

Every day after school, Hamad's uncle took him to visit the falcon. Hamad gave it a name, Najm, which means "star," because of a small white mark on its head. He helped the vet prepare its food and watched it grow stronger. "Don't forget," the vet reminded him one day, "Najm is wild. Soon you'll have to let him go."

On the day of the release, the whole family climbed a hill above the farm. Hamad held Najm on his arm, and his heart felt heavy. "Go on, my friend," he whispered, and he lifted his arm high. The falcon spread its wings and rose into the golden evening sky. Then, to everyone's surprise, it flew in three wide circles above Hamad's head before it disappeared over the mountains.

A week later, the vet phoned Hamad's grandfather with an unexpected offer. The clinic needed a young helper on weekends, and she wanted Hamad because he had shown so much patience and care. Hamad accepted immediately, and he never thought about the laptop again. Sometimes, when he works at the farm, he still sees a falcon with a small white mark circling high above him, as if it is saying thank you.

options: Caught in a wire fence on his grandfather's farm
Sitting on the roof of his house
Inside a cage in a man's car

options: To hide it from his grandfather

options: The man offered too little money

options: Because he had shown kindness and care for the falcon
Because he wanted to buy a laptop

pages.text: Every winter, Omar's family camped for a week in the desert, far away from the noise of the city. On the first evening, Grandfather pointed at the sky and said, "If you are ever lost, find the star that never moves." Omar, who was thirteen, smiled politely, but he was more interested in his phone. His younger sister Lina listened carefully and asked lots of questions.

The next afternoon, Uncle Khalid offered to take them to look for desert roses, beautiful stones that are made of sand. They drove for nearly an hour across the soft red dunes until they reached a group of dark rocks. The children ran around excitedly, and Lina soon found a small, perfect desert rose. "We should go back before sunset," said Uncle Khalid, looking at the sky.

As he was walking back to the car, Uncle Khalid slipped on the side of a dune and fell. When he tried to stand up, he cried out in pain because his right ankle was badly hurt. Omar and Lina helped him into the driver's seat, but he could only use his left foot. "I can drive slowly," he said bravely, "but you two will have to help me find the way."

By then, the sun had already disappeared and the air was getting cold. Omar checked his phone, but there was no signal and the battery was almost empty. Even worse, the wind had covered their tyre tracks with sand, so they could not follow them back. For a moment nobody spoke, and Omar felt his heart beating fast.

Then Omar remembered Grandfather's words, and suddenly they did not sound so boring anymore. "Our camp is north of here," he said. "Grandfather showed us how to find the North Star, the one called Al-Jadi." Lina nodded quickly. "First we find the seven bright stars that look like a big spoon, and then we follow the two stars at the end of it."

Unfortunately, thick clouds were moving across the sky and hiding most of the stars. They waited in the dark car, listening to the wind, and Lina held her brother's arm. After ten long minutes, the clouds moved away and the sky was suddenly full of light. "There it is!" shouted Lina, pointing at a small, steady star. "That's the one that never moves!"

Uncle Khalid drove very slowly while the children kept the star in front of the car. Once, a dune was too steep to climb, so they had to go around it and find the star again. Omar was in charge of the direction, and Lina watched for rocks in the headlights. Nobody complained, although they were all tired and hungry.

At last, they saw the orange light of a fire and heard the sound of a car horn in the distance. Their father ran towards them with a torch, and the whole family came to hug them. Later, sitting by the fire, Omar told Grandfather everything, and Lina gave him her desert rose as a present. Grandfather laughed and said, "You found something more valuable today, the way home." That night, Omar left his phone in the tent and spent a long time looking up at the stars.

questions.q: Why did Uncle Khalid need the children's help to drive back?
options: He had hurt his ankle and could not see the way in the dark.
He did not know how to drive a car.
He was too tired after looking for desert roses.

questions.q: Why couldn't they follow their tyre tracks back to the camp?
options: The wind had covered them with sand.
Another car had driven over them.

questions.q: In the story, what does the word "steady" mean when it describes the star?
How did Omar's feelings about Grandfather's advice change?
options: He first thought it was boring, but later he understood it was very useful.
He always thought it was the most important lesson.
He thought it was useful at first, but later he forgot it.

questions.q: Why do you think Omar left his phone in the tent at the end?
options: Because his father told him to stop using it.
Because he now found the stars more interesting and important.
Because he had lost the phone in the desert.

pages.text: Every summer, Omar and his younger sister Noura stayed with their grandfather in a small village on the Red Sea coast. Grandfather had been a fisherman for forty years, and he knew every rock and wave of the beach. One morning, while the sun was still low, Omar noticed strange marks in the sand. They looked like the tracks of a small car, going from the water to the dunes and back again.

"Those aren't car tracks," Grandfather said, kneeling down. "A green turtle came out of the sea last night to lay her eggs." Then he walked to a circle of white stones near the dunes. "And this is the nest she made almost two months ago. These babies could hatch any night now."

That evening, the family sat on the sand and waited. The stars came out one by one, and the only sounds were the waves and Noura's quiet questions. Then Omar saw something that worried him. Across the bay, a new café had opened, and its bright lights were shining over the beach. "Baby turtles find the sea by following the moonlight on the water," Grandfather explained, "so brighter lights can confuse them."

Just before midnight, the sand inside the circle began to move. First one tiny head appeared, then another, and soon dozens of baby turtles were climbing out of the nest. Noura covered her mouth so she wouldn't scream with excitement. But instead of going to the water, the turtles turned and started crawling slowly towards the café.

"They'll never reach the sea if they go that way," Omar said. "The crabs and birds will get them first." Grandfather thought for a moment. "Omar, you're the fastest runner in this family." "Go to the café and ask the owner to switch off his lights, just for one hour."

Omar ran along the beach as fast as he could, his heart beating loudly. The café owner, a young man called Faisal, was surprised to see a breathless boy at his door so late at night. When Omar explained, Faisal didn't argue. "I grew up here, and I've never seen turtles hatch," he said, reaching for the switch. "Of course I'll help."

Suddenly the beach went dark, and the moon's silver path on the water became clear again. Meanwhile, Noura and Grandfather had gently made a low wall of sand to stop the turtles from going further inland. One by one, the tiny animals changed direction and hurried towards the waves. Omar arrived back just in time to see the last baby disappear into the white foam.

The next week, Faisal put up new lights that were softer and pointed away from the beach. He also hung a sign on the café wall: "Quiet lights for turtle nights." Grandfather told Omar that only about one baby in a thousand grows up, but a female that survives will one day return to the same beach to lay her own eggs. Omar looked out at the dark sea and smiled. "Then we'll be here waiting for her," he said.

questions.q: What did Omar first think the marks in the sand were?
options: The tracks of a small car

questions.q: Why were the baby turtles going towards the café?
options: They were afraid of the waves

options: Unable to breathe easily after running

options: They carried the turtles to the sea

They called Faisal on the phone

options: He was angry that he had to change his lights

pages.text: It was almost midnight when the sky over the desert suddenly turned green. Rakan was sitting outside his uncle's camp with his cousin Noura, drinking warm tea. A ball of fire raced across the stars, as bright as the moon, then broke into pieces and disappeared behind the dunes. "Did you see that?" Noura whispered. "That wasn't a shooting star. It was much too big."

Uncle Sami came out of the tent, holding his phone. "People are posting videos from Riyadh, Al-Kharj and even Hofuf," he said. Rakan, who had read every book about space in his school library, felt his heart beating fast. "If it was a meteor, small rocks might have reached the ground," he explained. "And if we compare the videos, we could work out where they landed."

They spent the next morning sitting around a laptop. Noura drew lines on a map to show the direction of the fireball in each video. Where the lines crossed, there was a small area of sand and rock about forty kilometres from the camp. "Scientists do exactly the same thing," Rakan said proudly. "It's called triangulation."

Uncle Sami agreed to drive them there, but he had rules. "We stay together, we carry plenty of water, and we come back before the sun gets too hot," he said firmly. For two hours they walked slowly across the flat ground, looking for anything unusual. Most of the stones were pale and brown, and after a while Rakan began to lose hope.

Then Noura stopped. Half hidden in the sand lay a stone the size of a date, black and shiny, as if someone had burned it in an oven. She held a small magnet close to it, and the magnet jumped and stuck to its surface. "It's full of metal," she said, her voice shaking with excitement. "I think we've just found a piece of space."

Back in the city, Uncle Sami called a geology professor at the university. Dr. Huda examined the stone under a microscope while Rakan and Noura waited nervously. Finally she looked up and smiled. "You're right. This is a meteorite, and it has probably been travelling through space for about four and a half billion years."

Rakan could hardly believe it. The little rock in his hand was older than the mountains, older than the oceans, even older than Earth itself. Dr. Huda explained that studying it could help scientists understand how the planets were formed. "You have a choice," she said gently. "You can keep it, or you can let us study it here."

Noura and Rakan looked at each other, and they didn't need to say anything. They gave the meteorite to the university, and Dr. Huda promised to put their names on its label in the museum. That evening, back at the camp, they lay on the cold sand and watched the stars together. "Somewhere up there, more stones are waiting to fall," Noura said, and Rakan smiled. "Next time, we'll be ready."

questions.q: How did the children find the area where the stone might be?
options: They asked people in Riyadh to help them search.
They drew lines on a map using videos from different cities.
They followed the smoke from the fireball.

In the story, what does "examined" mean?
Why did Uncle Sami want to come back before the sun got too hot?
options: Because walking in the desert heat can be dangerous.
Because the meteorite would melt in the sun.

questions.q: What does the ending suggest about Rakan and Noura?
options: They are sad that they lost the meteorite.
They never want to look for meteorites again.
They are proud of their choice and excited to search again.

pages.text: Omar had waited all year for the school football final. But two weeks before the big day, he fell badly during training and broke his ankle. The doctor said he couldn't play for at least six weeks. That evening, Omar sat on his bed with his leg in plaster and stared sadly at his football boots.

The next day, Coach Khalid knocked on the door with a small blue notebook. "I still need you on this team," he said. "You can't run, but you have the sharpest eyes in the whole school." He explained that Al-Noor Academy, their opponents in the final, were playing a match on Thursday. "Go and watch them carefully, and write down everything you notice."

On Thursday, Omar's older brother Hamad drove him to the stadium. Omar sat in the stands and filled page after page: who was fast, who passed well, and who got tired after half time. Then he noticed something strange about Al-Noor's captain, number 9. Before he took a penalty, he bent down and touched his left sock, and then he shot to the right side of the goal.

At first, Omar thought it was just a habit or luck. So that night, with his father's permission, he watched videos of Al-Noor's old matches online. The captain had taken four penalties, and every time he did exactly the same thing. Omar smiled and closed the laptop. "Got you," he whispered.

On the day of the final, the stadium was full of families waving flags and cheering. Omar sat on the bench with his crutches beside him. Their goalkeeper, Saad, looked pale and nervous. "If they get a penalty, I'm finished," he said quietly. "Don't worry," Omar replied. "If that happens, just look at me."

The match was tough, and it was still 1-1 when the referee blew the final whistle. Now the winner would be decided by penalties. When the score was level, the Al-Noor captain walked forward to take his kick, and the whole crowd went silent. He bent down and touched his left sock. On the bench, Omar lifted his right hand high into the air.

Saad dived to the right and pushed the ball away with the tips of his fingers. The crowd went crazy! A moment later, their striker Ziyad stepped up and calmly scored the last penalty. They had won the final!

To everyone's surprise, the players ran straight past Saad and lifted Omar off the bench. "That save was half yours," Saad laughed. When Coach Khalid placed a medal around Omar's neck, he said, "Every great team needs a twelfth player." Omar looked at his little blue notebook and decided that next season he would play on the pitch and keep his eyes open too.

questions.q: Why couldn't Omar play in the final?
options: He was ill with a fever
He broke his ankle in training
His coach did not choose him

questions.q: What did the Al-Noor captain always do before taking a penalty?
In the story, what does "pale" mean when it describes Saad?
options: Having a white face because of fear

questions.q: Why did Omar lift his right hand during the penalties?
options: To ask the referee a question
To tell Saad which way to dive
To wave to his brother Hamad

questions.q: Why did Coach Khalid call Omar "a twelfth player"?
options: Because he helped the team win without playing on the pitch
Because his shirt number was twelve
Because he was the youngest player

pages.text: Lina and her younger sister Reem were spending the summer holidays at Aunt Huda's house in Al-Balad, the old part of Jeddah. The house was tall and narrow, with a beautiful wooden window called a rawshan that looked over a quiet street. On their first morning, Lina opened the window and found something strange on the windowsill. It was a small bird made of folded paper, sitting there as if it was waiting for her.

The next morning there was another paper bird, and the morning after that, there was a third. At night the girls heard a soft sound outside: tap, tap, tap. "It's a ghost," Reem whispered, pulling the blanket over her head. "Ghosts don't make paper birds," Lina said calmly, and she took out a notebook to write down every clue.

Lina carefully opened one of the birds and flattened the paper on the table. It was very old and yellow, and it was covered in neat handwriting in blue ink. There was a list of girls' names, and next to each name was a word like "good" or "excellent." "I think this is a page from an old school book," Lina said slowly. "But who would fold it into a bird, and why?"

That night the sisters decided to stay awake and watch. The street was so narrow that the house opposite seemed close enough to touch. Just after midnight, they saw a small light in the top window across the street. A wrinkled hand appeared, and a paper bird flew gently through the air and landed on their windowsill.

In the morning, the girls hurried to the little shop at the end of the street. "The house opposite yours?" said the kind shopkeeper. "That belongs to Umm Saad. She hurt her leg last year, so she rarely goes out now, and she walks with a stick." Lina looked at Reem and smiled. "So that explains the tapping sound," she said.

The next morning, the newest paper bird was waiting for them. Lina unfolded it with shaking hands, and her eyes grew wide. In the middle of the list, in the same blue ink, was a name they both knew: "Huda bint Ahmed — excellent." "That's Aunt Huda!" Reem shouted, and they ran downstairs to show her.

Aunt Huda read the page twice, and then her eyes filled with tears. "Umm Saad was my teacher when I was your age," she said quietly. "She was the one who made me love reading, but she moved away and I never saw her again. I had no idea she was living across the street!" She stood up at once and began preparing a plate of dates and a pot of Arabic coffee.

Umm Saad opened her door slowly, and when she saw Aunt Huda, her face lit up. "I recognised you weeks ago, but I was too shy to knock," she admitted. "I thought you had probably forgotten me, so I sent the pages from my old school register, hoping someone would notice." Aunt Huda held her teacher's hands and said, "How could I ever forget you?" From that day on, the girls visited Umm Saad every afternoon, and every evening they sent a paper bird back across the street.

questions.q: Where did Lina find the paper birds?
options: On the windowsill of the rawshan
At the door of the shop

questions.q: What was really making the "tap, tap, tap" sound at night?
In the story, the street is "narrow." What does "narrow" mean?
Why did Umm Saad send paper birds instead of knocking on the door?
options: She was too shy and thought Aunt Huda had forgotten her
She wanted to frighten the girls
She did not know anyone lived in the house

questions.q: How do you think Lina helped to solve the mystery?
options: She asked her aunt to tell her the answer
She stayed calm, looked for clues and watched carefully
She waited until the birds stopped coming

pages.text: When Yousef joined Khalid's class in Taif, nobody knew much about him. He sat by the window, drew pictures in his notebook and hardly ever spoke. On his first day, Khalid said hello to him twice, but Yousef didn't even look up. "He thinks he's better than us," Khalid told his friends at break.

A week later, the teacher put the two boys together for a science project about the famous Taif roses. Khalid wasn't happy, but he tried to be polite. "Shall we visit my uncle's rose farm on Saturday?" he asked, standing on Yousef's left. Again, Yousef said nothing, and Khalid felt his face go hot with anger.

Then Khalid walked round the desk and repeated the question, louder. This time Yousef turned and smiled. "Sorry," he said quietly. "I can't hear anything in my left ear. I've had this problem since I was little, and I hate telling people because they treat me differently." Khalid suddenly felt terrible about everything he had said.

From that day, Khalid always sat on Yousef's right, and the two boys started spending more time together. Yousef's drawings were amazing, and Khalid was good at explaining ideas, so their project quickly became the best in the class. Before the school trip to the mountains, Yousef showed Khalid a small mirror. "At my old school, I used this to send signals to my brother," he explained. "One flash means 'Where are you?' and two flashes mean 'I'm here.'"

On the trip, the class walked up a rocky path between the rose fields. Yousef stopped to draw a beautiful pink flower, while the others continued walking. When the teacher called everyone back to the bus, Khalid looked around and realised that his friend was missing. Shouting was useless, because the wind was strong and Yousef might not hear it anyway.

Khalid remembered the mirror. He borrowed the teacher's phone, turned on its light and pointed it at the hills: one flash, a pause, then another single flash. For a long minute, nothing happened. Then, far away near some old stone walls, two bright flashes shone back in the afternoon sun.

The teacher and Khalid hurried up the path and found Yousef sitting on a rock, holding his ankle. He had slipped while he was climbing down and had hurt his foot. "I knew someone would look for me," he said, "but I didn't know it would be you." Khalid laughed and helped him stand up. "Well, you taught me the code, didn't you?"

A week later, Yousef gave Khalid a present wrapped in brown paper. Inside was a drawing of two boys on a mountain, with a tiny light shining between them. Under it, Yousef had written: "Thank you for walking round the desk." Khalid put the drawing on his bedroom wall, and he still smiles every time he looks at it.

questions.q: Why didn't Yousef answer Khalid at the beginning of the story?
options: He couldn't hear with his left ear.
He thought he was better than Khalid.

questions.q: What did two flashes mean in Yousef's code?
In the story, what does "useless" mean in "Shouting was useless"?
Why did Yousef get left behind on the trip?
options: He stopped to draw a flower.

questions.q: What does Yousef's message "Thank you for walking round the desk" really show?
options: He was thankful that Khalid made the effort to understand him.
He wanted Khalid to change his seat in class.
He was happy that Khalid helped him tidy the classroom.

pages.text: Every summer, Nora left the heat of Riyadh and stayed with her grandfather in the mountains near Abha. She loved the cool air and the thick fog that covered the valley every morning. But this year, something was wrong. The well on Grandpa's farm was almost dry, and his pomegranate trees looked tired and thirsty.

"It hasn't rained properly for months," Grandpa said, touching a yellow leaf. "If the trees don't get water soon, we will lose them." Nora looked out at the white fog moving slowly between the trees. "Grandpa, there's water all around us," she said. "It's just floating in the air."

That night, Nora searched online and read about fog catchers. In dry places like Chile and Morocco, people hang large nets that collect tiny drops of water from the fog. The drops join together, become heavier and run down into a container. "If they can do it, so can I," she whispered, and she started drawing a plan in her notebook.

The next day, her cousin Faisal helped her build it. They used two wooden poles, an old plastic net from the market and a long pipe cut in half. By sunset, the fog catcher was standing proudly at the edge of the farm. Nora could hardly sleep because she was so excited.

In the morning, she ran outside, but her heart sank. A strong wind had blown all night, and the net lay on the ground, torn and dusty, with only a few drops in the bucket. "Maybe it was a silly idea," Nora said quietly. Faisal shook his head and said, "Scientists fail all the time. That's how they learn."

Nora sat under a tree, thinking. Then she noticed a spider's web between two branches, shining with tiny drops of water. The web was strong because it moved with the wind instead of fighting it, and its thin threads were very close together. "That's it!" she shouted. "We need a finer net, and it must be able to bend!"

This time they tied the net loosely with elastic ropes so it could move in the wind, and they used two layers of fine mesh. They also turned it towards the valley, where the fog was thickest. For three days, Nora checked the bucket every morning and wrote the results in her notebook. On the third morning, it was nearly full.

Grandpa poured the clear water around the roots of his favourite tree and smiled widely. "Your grandmother always said the clouds were a gift," he said. "Now you have found a way to catch them." When school started again, Nora presented her project at the science fair and won first prize. But the best prize came a month later: a photo from Grandpa of small green leaves on his pomegranate tree.

questions.q: Why were Grandpa's trees in danger?
options: It had not rained properly for months and the well was almost dry.
The fog was too cold for them.

options: A strong wind blew it down and tore the net.

pages.text: Every winter, Yousef's family drove to the edge of the Empty Quarter to camp under the stars. This year, Yousef had brought a new drone, a present for his thirteenth birthday. "Grandfather, I'm going to film the whole desert from the sky!" he said proudly. His grandfather poured the coffee and smiled. "The desert has been watching people for thousands of years," he said. "Be careful it doesn't film you."

That evening, around the fire, Grandfather told Yousef and his sister Layla about the singing dune. "When the wind is strong, one of the dunes here makes a deep sound, like a drum," he explained. Layla laughed and said, "Sand can't sing, Grandfather!" "You'll hear it one day," he replied calmly. "And if you ever get lost, listen for it, because it is always north of our camp."

The next morning, Yousef flew the drone over the red dunes while Layla watched the screen. Suddenly, a warning flashed: LOW BATTERY. The drone came down on top of a tall dune, very far away. "Dad told us not to go far," Layla said, but Yousef was already running. Sighing, she grabbed a bottle of water and followed him.

It took them almost an hour to reach the drone. Yousef picked it up and cheered, but Layla was staring at the horizon. A huge brown wall was moving towards them. "Sandstorm," she whispered. Within minutes, the wind was throwing sand into their faces, and the way back to the camp had disappeared.

They covered their faces with their scarves and sat down behind a large rock. "This is all my fault," Yousef said quietly. "I should have listened to Dad." "We can't change that now," Layla answered, "so let's think about what Grandfather told us." Then, through the noise of the wind, they heard something strange: a low, deep sound.

BOOM... BOOM... It was like a giant drum hidden under the sand. "The singing dune!" Layla shouted. "It's north of the camp, so we need to walk away from the sound!" They kept the deep noise behind them and walked slowly, holding hands so that they wouldn't get separated.

After what felt like hours, the wind began to drop. Through the dust, they saw lights flashing in the distance: it was their father's car. He ran towards them, his face pale with worry, and hugged them both tightly without saying a word. Behind him, Grandfather was standing by the tent, holding his cup of coffee as if nothing unusual had happened.

That night, Yousef apologized to his father and promised never to go off alone again. Then he showed everyone the video from the drone. The last few seconds showed two tiny figures walking in front of an enormous storm. "You see?" Grandfather said with a smile. "The desert filmed you after all."

stories.title: The Parrot Who Couldn't Keep a Secret

pages.text: When Grandpa left for Umrah, he gave Omar a very important job: looking after Captain, his grey parrot, for one week. "He's clever," Grandpa warned, "so be careful what you say near him." Omar laughed and promised to be careful. He had no idea how serious that warning was.

On the first evening, Omar was supposed to be doing his homework, but he was playing games on his tablet instead. When his mother called from the kitchen, he shouted, "I'm studying, Mama! Very hard!" A minute later, Captain shouted the same words in exactly the same voice. Then he added a loud electronic noise, just like Omar's game.

The next day, Omar heard that Aunt Huda was coming to visit. Aunt Huda was lovely, but she always ate all the best dates. "Quick, hide the dates!" Omar joked to his little sister, Lina. Captain was sitting on his perch, listening carefully with his head on one side.

That afternoon, Aunt Huda walked in with a big smile and a box of sweets. Before anyone could say hello, Captain flapped his wings and screamed, "Aunt Huda is coming! Quick, hide the dates!" The room went completely silent, and Omar's face turned as red as a tomato. Then Aunt Huda burst out laughing so loudly that the parrot almost fell off his perch.

By Wednesday, Captain had learned new tricks. He copied the doorbell perfectly, so Omar's father kept opening the door to nobody. He also copied Mama's phone ringtone, and the whole family searched under cushions for a phone that wasn't ringing. "This bird is driving me crazy," Dad complained, but he was trying not to smile.

On Friday evening, it was time to collect Grandpa from the airport, but Dad couldn't find his car keys anywhere. Everyone looked in pockets, drawers and even the rubbish bin. "We're going to be late!" Dad groaned, checking his watch for the tenth time. Suddenly Captain cleared his throat in a very familiar way.

"Keys next to the milk, keys next to the milk," Captain said in Dad's own deep voice. Everyone stared at each other, and then Omar ran to the fridge and opened it. There, beside the milk, were the car keys, nice and cold! Dad had put them there while he was talking on the phone and had completely forgotten.

At the airport, Grandpa hugged everyone and asked, "So, did Captain behave himself?" Before Omar could answer, Captain shouted, "I'm studying, Mama! Hide the dates!" Grandpa raised his eyebrows and looked at Omar, who shrugged and grinned. "Well," Grandpa said, laughing, "it seems he learned a lot this week, and I wonder who his teacher was!"

pages.text: Every Friday evening, Faisal's grandfather told the same story. "When I was young, I saw a creature in the sea with the face of a gentle old man," he said. "It ate grass under the water, like a camel in the desert." Faisal, who was thirteen, always laughed politely. "Grandpa, there are no cows in the sea," he said, but his grandfather only smiled and drank his tea.

That summer, Faisal's uncle Khalid, a marine biologist, invited him on a research trip near the Farasan Islands. Their job was to study the seagrass that grew on the bottom of the Red Sea. "Seagrass is like a forest for the ocean," Uncle Khalid explained while he checked the diving equipment. "Small fish hide in it, and turtles feed on it." Faisal put on his life jacket and felt more excited than he had ever felt before.

For three days, they snorkelled, took photos and wrote careful notes. On the fourth afternoon, as they were returning to the island, the engine made a terrible noise and stopped. Uncle Khalid tried again and again, but nothing happened. "Don't worry," he said calmly. "I've called the coast guard on the radio, and they'll be here in about two hours."

The sun began to go down, and the water turned orange and gold. Faisal sat on the edge of the boat and watched the quiet waves. Suddenly, he heard a soft breathing sound behind him. He turned slowly and saw a large grey head with small eyes and a round nose. It came up out of the water, took a deep breath and disappeared again.

"Uncle! Something is down there!" Faisal shouted. Uncle Khalid grabbed his torch, and when he looked into the water, his voice shook. "Faisal, that's a dugong. People also call it a sea cow, and there are very few left in the Red Sea. I've worked here for ten years, and I've never seen one!" Then a smaller head appeared next to the first, a baby staying close to its mother.

But Faisal noticed something else floating towards them: an old fishing net, as wide as a car. The dugongs were feeding right in its path. "If they get caught, they could drown," Uncle Khalid said. "Dugongs have to breathe air, just like us." Without another word, they picked up the long poles from the boat and leaned over the side.

It was hard work, because the net was heavy with seaweed and their arms soon hurt. Little by little, they pulled it out of the water and onto the boat. Below them, the mother and her baby swam calmly away into the dark seagrass. By the time the lights of the coast guard boat appeared, Faisal was tired and wet, but he couldn't stop smiling.

A week later, Uncle Khalid's photos helped to make the seagrass area a protected zone. On Friday evening, Grandfather began his story again: "When I was young, I saw a creature in the sea..." This time, Faisal finished it for him. "...with the face of a gentle old man," he said with a smile, "and so have I!" Grandfather laughed so hard that he almost dropped his tea.

stories.title: The Girl Who Caught the Clouds

pages.text: Every morning in Abha, thick white fog rolled down the mountains and covered Layla's village. Her grandmother called it "the clouds coming to visit." But that summer, the rain had not come, and Grandma's little garden of herbs and roses was slowly dying. "If only we could drink the fog," Layla said as she watched it drift past the window.

That afternoon, her science teacher, Ms. Huda, announced the school invention competition. "Your invention must solve a real problem in your community," she explained. Layla's heart started beating faster, because she already knew which problem she wanted to solve. On the way home, she noticed tiny drops of water shining on a spider's web.

For the next two weeks, Layla spent every evening in the yard with her younger brother, Faisal. They tied a large plastic net between two wooden poles and put a gutter underneath to collect the drops. "Are you sure this will work?" Faisal asked, holding the hammer. "Spiders have been doing it for millions of years," Layla replied with a smile.

The next morning, they ran outside before breakfast, but the bucket held only a few sad drops. Worse, the strong mountain wind had torn the net in two places. Layla sat down on the cold step and felt like giving up. "Maybe the competition isn't for people like me," she whispered.

Grandma came out with two cups of hot tea and sat down beside her. She didn't say anything at first; she just looked at the broken net. Then she went inside and returned with an old basket she had woven many years ago. "Look how the threads cross each other," she said. "When I was young, we learned that small, tight weaving is stronger than one big, loose piece."

Suddenly, Layla had an idea. Together, they wove a new net from thin threads, with tiny holes like Grandma's basket, so more drops could catch on it. Faisal suggested making the frame lower and putting it at an angle, so the wind would pass through it instead of tearing it. The next morning, the bucket was almost half full of clear, cold water.

On the day of the competition, the hall was full of robots, apps and flashing lights. Layla's fog net looked very simple next to them, and she felt nervous as the judges walked over. But when she explained how one net could water a whole garden without electricity, the judges stopped writing and listened carefully. "Who taught you to weave like this?" one judge asked. "My grandmother," Layla answered proudly.

Layla didn't win first prize, but she won the award for the most useful invention, and the town council asked her to build three more nets for the village school. Weeks later, Grandma's roses were blooming again, and the herbs smelled stronger than ever. Every morning, when the fog rolled down the mountains, Layla smiled. The clouds were still coming to visit, but now they brought a gift.

pages.text: The plane landed in Kuala Lumpur just after sunrise, and Yousef pressed his face to the window. Green hills stretched as far as he could see, and heavy clouds were hanging over them. "Welcome to Malaysia," his father said with a smile. It was the family's first trip to Asia, and Yousef had been counting the days for months.

At the baggage area, hundreds of suitcases were moving slowly along the belt. "There's ours!" shouted his younger sister, Lina, pointing at a dark green case. Yousef pulled it off quickly, and the family hurried outside to find a taxi. Nobody noticed that the case was a little heavier than usual.

At the hotel, Yousef opened the suitcase to find his phone charger. Instead of his clothes, he saw an old camera, a pile of paintbrushes and a notebook with a leather cover. "This isn't ours!" he cried. His mother's face went pale, because all their clothes and the presents for their cousins were in their own case.

His father called the airport, but the woman on the phone could not help much. "Many passengers have green suitcases, sir," she said. "If the owner contacts us, we will let you know." Yousef sat on the bed and opened the notebook, hoping to find a name or an address. It was full of beautiful drawings of mosques, markets and mountains from all over the world.

On the last page, Yousef found something important: a train ticket tucked inside the cover. "Look! The owner is going to Penang tomorrow at eight o'clock, from KL Sentral station," he said. "If we get there early, we might catch him." His father looked at him for a moment and then nodded. "You'd make a good detective," he laughed.

The next morning, the station was busy and noisy, and Yousef's heart was beating fast. People were rushing in every direction, pulling bags behind them. Then Lina grabbed his arm. An old man was standing near platform three, holding a dark green suitcase exactly like theirs, and he looked very confused.

"Excuse me, sir, I think you have our bag," Yousef said politely. The man opened it, saw Lina's pink scarf on top, and began to laugh. "And you have my whole life's work!" he said, holding his notebook as if it were treasure. His name was Mr. Tan, and he had been travelling and painting for forty years.

Before his train left, Mr. Tan tore a drawing out of his notebook and gave it to Yousef. It showed a boy with a green suitcase, standing in a crowded station. "A good traveller doesn't only look at places," he said. "He also notices the small things." That evening, Yousef's mother tied a bright red ribbon around their suitcase, and Yousef started a travel notebook of his own.

pages.text: Hamad had never been the best player in his neighbourhood, but he knew the rules of football better than anyone. Whenever his friends argued about a foul, they always turned to him for the answer. So when the youth league in Jeddah needed young referees, his coach suggested that he should take the training course. Six weeks later, Hamad proudly received his first black shirt and a shiny silver whistle.

For months, he refereed small matches between younger children on Friday afternoons. Then one evening, the league manager phoned him with surprising news. "The under-14 final needs a referee, and we've chosen you," he said. Hamad was delighted until he heard the names of the two teams. His older brother, Saad, was the captain of Al-Noor Academy, one of the finalists.

"Are you sure that's a good idea?" asked his mother at dinner. Saad laughed and put a heavy hand on Hamad's shoulder. "Don't worry, Mum. He'll be on our side, won't you, little brother?" Hamad smiled politely, but he lay awake for hours that night, staring at the ceiling.

On the day of the final, the stadium was full of families waving flags and cheering loudly. The match was fast and exciting, and Hamad ran up and down the pitch, watching every move carefully. By the second half, the score was 1-1. With only five minutes left, the crowd was on its feet, and everyone was hoping for a winning goal.

Suddenly, a striker from the other team dribbled past two defenders and raced into the penalty area. Saad rushed back and stretched out his leg, and the striker crashed to the ground. The whole stadium went silent, and every head turned towards Hamad. He had seen it clearly: Saad had tripped him, and he hadn't touched the ball at all.

Hamad took a deep breath, blew his whistle hard and pointed to the penalty spot. Saad's teammates surrounded him, shouting angrily, while Saad just stared at his brother in shock. Hamad's hands were shaking, but he calmly showed Saad a yellow card. A moment later, the striker scored, and the score became 2-1.

Al-Noor attacked again and again, but they couldn't find another goal before the final whistle. The other team celebrated wildly, and some Al-Noor fans booed as Hamad left the pitch. He felt sick as he walked towards the tunnel. He kept wondering whether he had just lost his brother's friendship forever.

Saad was waiting for him by the changing room, still wearing his muddy shirt. "I tripped him," he admitted quietly. "You made the right decision, and I'm proud of you." Behind them, the league manager smiled and said Hamad would referee even bigger matches next season. Saad laughed and added, "Next time, I'll keep my feet to myself!"
