stories.title: The Robot That Would Not Clean

pages.text: Every summer, the dust in Al-Ahsa covered the solar panels on Grandfather's farmhouse roof like a thin brown blanket. When the panels were dirty, they made less electricity, and Grandfather had to climb up and clean them by hand. This year, Reem had a better idea. For three months, she had been building a small robot that could clean the panels by itself, and she was going to show it at her school science fair.

She called the robot Sahm, which means 'arrow', because she hoped it would be fast. On the first test, Sahm rolled smoothly along the roof, and its soft brushes swept the dust away. Grandfather clapped from the yard below. But when Sahm reached the last panel, it suddenly stopped and refused to move.

Reem and her younger brother Omar spent the whole evening checking the program on her laptop. 'There's nothing wrong with the code,' Omar complained. 'Maybe your robot is just lazy.' Grandfather smiled and poured them some tea. 'Sometimes a problem is really a message,' he said quietly. 'You just have to learn how to read it.'

Early the next morning, Reem climbed the ladder and looked carefully under the edge of the last panel. Hidden in the shadow, there was a tiny nest with three pale eggs, and a small brown bird was watching her nervously. Suddenly, Reem understood. Weeks ago, she had programmed Sahm to stop whenever its sensor noticed something warm, so it would never hurt a cat or a person's hand.

'The science fair is in two days,' Omar said when she told him. 'If you remove the heat sensor, Sahm will work perfectly.' Reem thought about it for a long time, but finally she shook her head. 'It is working perfectly,' she replied. 'It's doing exactly what I asked it to do.'

At the fair, the judges watched Sahm clean a row of dusty panels, and then it stopped in front of a warm cup of tea that Reem had placed there. One judge frowned and asked why her robot had given up. Reem explained about the nest, the eggs and the sensor. 'A machine that is very good at its job can still be dangerous,' she said. 'I wanted Sahm to be careful too.'

When the results were announced, Reem didn't win first place, because another student had built a faster robot. However, the judges gave her a special prize for 'Best Design for People and Nature'. Omar cheered louder than anyone in the hall. 'Okay,' he admitted on the way home, 'your robot isn't lazy. It's polite.'

Three weeks later, the eggs hatched, and soon the little birds were flying around the palm trees. Reem added a new part to Sahm's program: if it found a nest, it would send a message to her phone instead of just waiting. Now, every morning, Sahm cleans the roof while Grandfather drinks his tea in the yard. And whenever it stops, the whole family knows it has found something worth protecting.

pages.text: Every Saturday, Lina helped her grandfather in his small workshop in Al-Balad, the old part of Jeddah. Grandpa Saleh was a carpenter, and he repaired the wooden windows called roshans on the tall coral-stone houses. Some of these houses were more than two hundred years old. "These windows have watched our city grow," he often said. Lina thought it was just one of his stories.

One morning, a team brought a broken roshan into the workshop. It had come from Bayt Nour, an old house that was being restored by the city. While Grandpa was removing a cracked panel, something fell onto the floor. It was a folded piece of paper, yellow and as thin as a dry leaf. "Careful," Grandpa whispered. "That might be older than me."

Lina opened it slowly. The handwriting was beautiful but hard to read, and the date showed it was written about a hundred years ago. Grandpa read it aloud: "My dear son Hamza, if the ship from India does not return, look behind the third coral stone by the well. What I have saved is for you and for this house." Lina's heart was beating fast. "Grandpa, do you think it's still there?"

The next day, they went to Bayt Nour with Mr. Adel, the engineer in charge of the work. The house smelled of dust and sea salt, and thin lines of light came through the old wood. In the courtyard, they found an old well that had been covered with a metal sheet. Mr. Adel read the letter and frowned. "We must be careful. These stones can't be replaced easily."

They counted the stones around the well. The first and second were solid, but when Grandpa tapped the third, it sounded hollow. With Mr. Adel's permission, they removed it slowly with soft tools. Behind it was a small space, and inside was a wooden box wrapped in cloth. Lina held her breath as Grandpa lifted the lid.

There was no gold inside. Instead, there was a notebook, a small brass compass and some old photos of men standing next to a ship. At first, Lina felt disappointed. Then she turned the pages and saw long lists of goods: coffee from Yemen, spices from India and cloth for the pilgrims who arrived at the port. "This is exactly what historians dream of," Mr. Adel said quietly.

Over the next few weeks, Lina helped a researcher from the university read the notebook. They learned that the merchant, Abdullah Nour, had lost his ship in a storm. However, his son Hamza had kept the family business going and had even paid to repair the mosque nearby. Every page showed how hard people had worked to make Jeddah a city that welcomed travellers from all over the world.

When Bayt Nour opened to visitors the following year, the box, the compass and the letter were displayed in a glass case. Next to them was a sign: "Discovered by Saleh and Lina, carpenters." Lina smiled, because she had never called herself a carpenter before. That evening, she touched a roshan in the workshop and said, "You were right, Grandpa. These windows really do remember."

pages.text: Lina had always thought the Farasan Islands were just a dot on the map. But now, standing on the white sand with the Red Sea shining in front of her, she understood why Uncle Khalid loved his job here. He was a ranger, and his work was to protect the islands' wildlife. "Tonight, if we're lucky, you'll see something amazing," he told Lina and her younger brother, Faisal.

That evening, Uncle Khalid led them along a quiet beach, far from the town. He stopped next to a small circle of sticks in the sand. "Two months ago, a green turtle laid more than a hundred eggs here," he whispered. "They should hatch any day now." Faisal knelt down and stared at the sand, as if he expected it to move immediately.

They waited for almost two hours. The moon rose slowly over the water, and the waves made a soft, calm sound. Lina was beginning to feel sleepy when she noticed something strange: the sand inside the circle was sinking. Then a tiny flipper appeared, followed by a small dark head.

Within minutes, dozens of baby turtles were climbing out of the nest. They were no bigger than Lina's palm, but they moved with surprising energy. "They use the moonlight on the sea to find their way," Uncle Khalid explained. But instead of heading towards the water, the baby turtles began crawling in the opposite direction.

Lina turned around and saw bright lights shining on a hill behind the beach. A group of men had set up a camp there, with a large lamp and a car with its headlights on. "The turtles think those lights are the sea," Uncle Khalid said, his voice worried. "If they go that way, they'll get lost, and birds or crabs will catch them before morning."

"I'll go and ask them to switch off the lights," Lina said, and she ran up the hill before anyone could stop her. Her heart was beating fast as she reached the camp, where three men were drinking tea. She took a deep breath and explained the problem politely. The oldest man listened carefully, then stood up. "We didn't know," he said. "Of course we'll help."

One by one, the lights went dark. Meanwhile, Faisal and Uncle Khalid knelt on the sand and gently made a path with their hands, without touching the turtles. Slowly, the baby turtles turned around and moved towards the silver line of the sea. The men from the camp came down to watch, and nobody said a word.

When the last tiny turtle disappeared into the waves, Faisal let out a happy shout. "Only about one in a thousand will grow up," Uncle Khalid said quietly, "but tonight you gave all of them a chance." The oldest man shook Lina's hand and promised to tell other campers about the turtles. As they walked home under the stars, Lina realised that sometimes protecting nature simply means knowing when to turn off the lights.

questions.q: What was Uncle Khalid's job on the Farasan Islands?
options: He was a ranger who protected wildlife.

questions.q: Why did the baby turtles move in the wrong direction at first?

options: Small, simple actions can make a big difference to nature.

pages.text: On Friday, the whole family was coming to Lina's house for lunch. Twenty people were expected, including Grandma Noura, who was famous for the best kabsa in the family. Lina's mother had flown to Jeddah to visit her sister and was planning to return early that morning. "Don't worry," she had said on the phone the night before. "I'll be home by nine, and we'll cook together."

At eight o'clock, Lina's phone rang. "There's a sandstorm here, and all the flights have been delayed," her mother said. "I won't get home before two." Lunch was at one. Lina's father looked at the empty kitchen and said, "I can make tea... and that's all I can make."

Lina's younger brother, Omar, started to panic, but Lina opened the kitchen drawer and took out an old notebook. Inside, in Grandma Noura's careful handwriting, was a recipe for kabsa for twenty people. "We can do this," Lina said, although her hands were shaking a little. She gave everyone a job, and soon Omar was chopping onions with tears running down his face.

Lina measured the spices exactly: cardamom, cloves, cinnamon and two dried black limes. As the chicken cooked with the onions and tomatoes, a wonderful smell filled the whole house. Everything was going well until Lina read the last line of the recipe. It didn't say how many minutes the rice needed. It just said, "Cook until the rice tells you it's ready."

Lina tried to call her mother, but the signal at the airport was too weak. "How can rice tell you anything?" Omar asked, confused. Lina closed her eyes and remembered standing next to her grandmother years ago. "Listen and watch," Grandma had said. "When the bubbling becomes quiet and small holes appear on top, the rice is speaking to you."

At a quarter to one, the doorbell rang, and the house quickly filled with aunts, uncles and cousins. Grandma Noura walked slowly into the kitchen and smelled the air. Without a word, she lifted the lid of the big pot and looked inside. Lina held her breath while her grandmother picked up a spoon.

Grandma tasted the rice and chewed it slowly for what felt like a very long time. "A little more salt next time," she said at last, "but this is my kabsa." Then she smiled and touched Lina's cheek. "I never wrote the cooking time because every pot and every fire is different. A real cook doesn't follow the clock. She pays attention."

When Lina's mother finally arrived at three, tired and dusty, a warm plate was waiting for her. She ate every grain of rice and laughed when she heard the whole story. Before Grandma Noura left, she put the old notebook into Lina's hands. "This belongs to the next cook in the family," she said, and Omar shouted from the living room, "Next time, I'm making the dessert!"

questions.q: Why couldn't Lina's mother come home in time to cook?
options: Her flight was delayed because of a sandstorm.
She was busy helping her sister with lunch.
She forgot about the family lunch.

questions.q: What did Lina find in the kitchen drawer?
options: A list of the guests' names

questions.q: In the story, what does the word "panic" mean?
options: To feel suddenly very worried and afraid

questions.q: How did Lina know when the rice was ready?
options: She finally reached her mother on the phone.
She set a timer for twenty minutes.
She remembered her grandmother's advice to listen and watch.

questions.q: Why do you think Grandma Noura gave the notebook to Lina?
options: She believed Lina had become a real cook who could continue the family recipes.
She didn't want to cook anymore.
She was angry that Lina used too little salt.

pages.text: Faris had a secret under his bed: an old oud wrapped in a blanket. It used to belong to his grandfather, who played it every Friday evening on the roof of their house in Taif. Grandfather had passed away two years ago, and since then nobody had touched it. One of the strings was broken, and the wood had a long crack near the top.

When Mr. Hamdan announced the school's Heritage Evening, Faris's classmates were excited. "Everyone can perform something: a poem, a story or music," the teacher said. Faris's best friend, Yousef, was planning to play his electric keyboard with big speakers. "You should play your grandfather's oud," Yousef said, but Faris shook his head and replied, "It's broken, and I've forgotten the song."

That evening, his grandmother noticed that he looked sad. When he told her why, she disappeared into her room and came back with a small box of old cassette tapes. "Your grandfather sometimes recorded himself," she said with a smile. "Maybe the song is still here." They found an old cassette player in the cupboard, and after a lot of crackling, a gentle melody filled the room.

The next morning, Faris took the oud to a small music shop in the old market. The owner, an old man with careful hands, examined the crack for a long time. "This instrument has been loved for many years," he said. "I can repair it, but you must practise every day, because an oud gets lonely if nobody plays it." For three weeks, Faris practised after his homework, listening to the tape again and again until his fingers hurt.

On the night of the Heritage Evening, the school hall was full of parents and students. Faris was the last performer, and his hands were shaking. Yousef was in the middle of his keyboard piece when suddenly all the lights went out. The air conditioning stopped, the speakers went silent, and people began to whisper nervously in the dark.

"The electricity will be back in a few minutes!" Mr. Hamdan called, but nobody could hear him clearly. Faris held his oud tightly, and then he realised something important: his instrument didn't need any electricity at all. Someone switched on a phone torch to light the stage. Taking a deep breath, Faris walked slowly towards it.

He sat down and began to play his grandfather's melody. At first the notes were quiet, but soon they filled the whole hall. People stopped whispering, and more phone lights appeared around the room like small stars. In the front row, his grandmother closed her eyes and listened with a peaceful smile.

When the song ended, the lights came back on, and the hall exploded with applause. Yousef ran to hug him, laughing, "You saved the whole evening!" Later, at home, Grandmother put the oud back in its place. This time it wasn't under the bed, but on the living room wall where everyone could see it. "Your grandfather's song isn't finished, and now it's yours to continue," she said.

questions.q: Where did Faris keep the oud at the start of the story?
How did Faris remember his grandfather's song?
options: His teacher taught it to him
He listened to an old cassette tape
Yousef played it on the keyboard

questions.q: What does the word "repair" mean in the story?
options: To fix something that is broken

questions.q: Why could Faris play when the lights went out?
options: His oud did not need electricity
The school turned on a generator

questions.q: Why did Grandmother put the oud on the wall at the end?
options: Because Faris did not want to play anymore
Because she was proud and wanted the oud to be seen and played

pages.text: Every Friday, the whole family met at Grandfather's house in Taif. The best thing in his sitting room was an old brass compass. It had belonged to his own father, a traveller who crossed the desert with camels. Faisal was twelve and read detective stories every night, and he loved to hold the compass and imagine those long journeys. But this Friday, when he went to the shelf after lunch, the compass was gone.

"Someone must have taken it," Faisal said to his cousin Noura. Noura was thirteen and very sensible, and she looked around the room carefully. "Or maybe Grandfather moved it," she said. But Grandfather shook his head sadly. "I saw it there this morning," he said.

Faisal immediately thought of their little cousin Omar, who was eight and always asked to play with the compass. "He was alone in this room before lunch," Faisal whispered. "I'm sure he hid it." Noura frowned. "A good detective needs evidence, not just a feeling," she said.

So they started to search for clues. The window next to the shelf was wide open, and there were small scratches on the wooden frame. On the carpet below, Noura found a shiny black feather. Faisal picked up a piece of bread with tiny holes in it, as if something had been pecking at it.

Just then, Omar came in, holding his toy car. "Did you take Grandfather's compass?" Faisal asked, a little too loudly. Omar's eyes filled with tears. "No! I was helping Grandmother in the kitchen all morning," he said, and Grandmother, who was standing at the door, agreed. Faisal felt his face turn hot, and he said sorry to his cousin.

Noura held up the feather. "I think our thief can fly," she said. Grandmother laughed. "That's the crow from the palm tree," she explained. "Every morning I put bread out for it on the windowsill." Faisal remembered reading that crows are very clever and sometimes collect shiny objects.

The three cousins hurried into the garden and looked up at the tall palm tree. High among the leaves, they could see a messy nest made of sticks. Their uncle brought a ladder and climbed up carefully while the crow complained loudly from the roof. When he came down, his hands were full: the compass, two teaspoons, a silver key and a gold ring.

"My ring!" cried Aunt Huda. "I lost it here last summer!" Everyone laughed, and Grandfather put the compass safely in a glass box. That evening, Faisal wrote in his notebook: "Case closed. Thief: one crow. Lesson: look for evidence before you blame someone." Then he gave Omar the first turn to hold the compass, and put some bread on the windowsill for the clever crow.

questions.q: Who did the compass first belong to?
options: The uncle who climbed the ladder

questions.q: Why did Faisal first think Omar had taken the compass?
options: Omar had a black feather in his pocket
Omar loved the compass and was alone in the room before lunch
Omar was standing next to the open window

questions.q: In the story, what does "evidence" mean?
options: Facts or things that show what really happened

questions.q: Why did the crow often come to Grandfather's window?
options: Grandmother put bread out for it every morning
It wanted to look at the compass

questions.q: What can we guess about Faisal at the end of the story?
options: He is still angry with Omar
He feels sorry he blamed Omar and wants to be kind to him
He wants to catch the crow and keep it

pages.text: Everyone in Faris's class had watched the videos of the Silver Falcon, the mysterious hero who flew over the city at night. Omar wanted to fly like him, and Yusuf dreamed of having super strength. Faris had a power too, but he had never told anyone, because it seemed a bit silly. Whenever he touched a broken machine, he could hear it whisper exactly what was wrong.

It had started last summer, when his grandmother's old radio suddenly stopped working. As soon as Faris picked it up, he heard a tiny, tired voice: "A wire is loose near my battery." He carefully opened the back, found the wire, and the radio began to play again. Since then, he had fixed a fan, two bicycles and his uncle's coffee machine, but nobody knew how he did it.

One Thursday, the school was getting ready for its science fair when the sky turned a strange orange colour. "A sandstorm is coming," Mr. Hamdan announced. "Nobody is allowed to leave the building until it passes." Within minutes, the wind was screaming against the windows, and then, with a loud click, all the lights went out.

The students were moved into the sports hall, where it was dark and getting hotter every minute. Some of the younger children began to cry, and their teachers tried to keep them calm. Abu Saleh, the school caretaker, came in with sweat running down his face. "The emergency generator won't start," he said quietly to Mr. Hamdan. "I've tried everything I know."

Faris's heart was beating fast. If he helped, everyone would ask questions, and he might have to explain his secret. But when he looked at the frightened little children, he knew he couldn't just sit there and do nothing. He stood up and said, "Abu Saleh, could I have a look at the generator, please?" Omar laughed nervously and whispered, "You're not the Silver Falcon, you know!"

In the small room behind the hall, the generator stood huge and silent. Faris placed his hand on its warm metal side and closed his eyes. This time the voice was deep and slow: "Air... I cannot breathe... my filter is full of sand." Faris explained this to Abu Saleh, and while Omar held his phone light, the two of them took out the filter and shook the sand away.

Abu Saleh pressed the button, and the engine coughed once, twice, and then roared to life. The lights came back on, cool air began to flow, and the whole hall burst into cheers. Mr. Hamdan looked at Faris with surprise and asked, "How on earth did you know what was wrong?" Faris just smiled and replied, "I listened very carefully."

The following week, Faris presented his science fair project, "How Sandstorms Damage Machines", and won first prize. "Maybe you really are a superhero," Omar said, giving him a friendly push. Faris thought about it as he walked home. Some heroes fly through the sky, but others simply listen when everyone else is shouting, and that evening, his grandmother's radio sang more cheerfully than ever.

questions.q: What was Faris's special power?
options: He could fly over the city at night.
He could hear broken machines say what was wrong.
He was stronger than anyone at school.

questions.q: Why did the lights go out at school?
options: The science fair used too much electricity.

questions.q: What was wrong with the generator?
options: A wire was loose near the battery.
Its filter was full of sand.

questions.q: In the story, "frightened" children are children who are...
Why did Faris decide to help even though he wanted to keep his secret?
options: He wanted to win first prize at the science fair.
He wanted to be more famous than the Silver Falcon.
He cared more about the scared children than about his secret.

pages.text: Faisal's family drove for three hours before they finally stopped among the red sand dunes north of Riyadh. While Dad and Grandfather put up the big tent, Faisal held his phone high in the air, walking in circles. "There's no signal anywhere," he complained. His sister Noura laughed and threw him a tent pole. "Good. Now you can actually help."

After dinner, Grandfather built a small fire and made sweet tea with mint. The sky was so dark that Faisal could see thousands of stars, more than he had ever seen in the city. "Before phones, we used these to find our way," Grandfather said, pointing up. "That bright one is Al-Jadi, the North Star. If you know where it is, you will never get lost in the desert."

Later that night, Faisal couldn't sleep, so he went outside with Noura to look at the stars again. Suddenly, Noura grabbed his arm. Far away, behind the dunes, a tiny light was flashing: three short flashes, three long flashes, then three short ones again. "That's a message," Faisal whispered. "We learned it at school. It means someone needs help!"

They ran to wake Dad and Grandfather, who listened carefully and then looked at the light for a long moment. "It's at least two kilometres away," Dad said, worried. "Without a signal, how will we find our way back?" Grandfather smiled and pointed at the sky. "We have the North Star. Faisal, you will be my navigator tonight."

Dad drove slowly across the sand while Faisal watched the North Star through the window and told him when to turn. Every few minutes, the flashing light appeared again, closer each time. At last, the car lights showed a small white car at the bottom of a dune. Its wheels were deep in the soft sand, and a man and a young boy were standing beside it, holding a torch.

"Thank God you came," the man said, and his voice was shaking. His name was Mr. Saleh, and he had taken his son Omar to see the desert, but they had got stuck at sunset. Their phones had no battery left, and they had only one small bottle of water. Grandfather gave Omar some water and put a warm blanket around his shoulders.

Grandfather explained what to do. First, they let some air out of the tyres so the wheels could hold the sand better. Then everyone dug around the wheels with their hands and pushed while Mr. Saleh drove. On the third try, the car moved forward, and Omar cheered so loudly that Noura started laughing.

Mr. Saleh and Omar followed them back to camp, where they all shared tea and dates until the sky turned orange. "If you hadn't seen my light, I don't know what would have happened," Mr. Saleh said quietly. Later, when the others were asleep, Faisal noticed that he hadn't checked his phone once all night. He looked up at the last stars disappearing in the morning sky and smiled, because now he knew they had been talking to him all along.

What did the flashing light mean?
In the story, what does the word "stuck" mean?
How did Faisal help the family find their way in the desert?
options: He used a map on his phone.
He followed car tracks in the sand.

questions.q: What does the ending suggest about Faisal?
options: He wants to go home quickly.
He now values the stars and what Grandfather taught him.
He is still angry about having no signal.

pages.text: Yousef had a secret: he was terrified of speaking in front of people. In class he often knew the answers, but he kept his hand down and his eyes on his desk. So when Mr. Hamdan announced that every student in Year 8 would present the morning assembly once this term, Yousef's stomach dropped. His turn was on Thursday.

For a whole week, he practised every break in the empty storeroom behind the gym. He had written a short talk about his grandfather, who had planted fifty palm trees in his village. But each time he read it aloud, his voice sounded small and shaky, like a radio with weak batteries. One afternoon, he heard someone clapping slowly behind him.

It was Uncle Saleh, the school caretaker, holding a broom. "You're speaking to the floor," he said kindly. "Look up. Speak to the person in the last row, not the first. If they can hear you, everyone can." Yousef laughed nervously, but the next day he tried it, and his voice filled the little room.

On Thursday morning, three hundred students stood in lines in the courtyard. Yousef walked to the microphone, his papers trembling in his hand. He took a deep breath and opened his mouth, and at that exact moment, the speakers went silent. The electricity had cut out across the whole school.

Some boys at the back started whispering, and a few of them laughed. Mr. Hamdan was already hurrying towards the office to check the power. Yousef could have walked away, and nobody would have blamed him. Then he saw Uncle Saleh standing by the gate, at the very end of the courtyard, and the old man lifted his chin, just a little.

Yousef put the papers in his pocket. He didn't need them, because he had practised so many times that he knew every word. He looked straight at Uncle Saleh and began: "My grandfather planted fifty palm trees, and people told him he was wasting his time." His voice travelled across the courtyard, clear and strong, and the whispering stopped.

He told them how his grandfather had carried water in heavy buckets for years, and how most of the trees had died in the first summer. "But he kept going," Yousef said, "because he believed that small efforts grow into something big." When he finished, there was a moment of complete silence. Then the whole courtyard burst into applause, and even the boys at the back were clapping.

Later, the head teacher shook his hand and asked him to join the school's speaking team. As Yousef walked back to class, he passed Uncle Saleh, who was sweeping the courtyard as usual. "Last row?" the old man asked with a smile. "Last row," Yousef replied, and for the first time all year, he didn't look at the floor.

questions.q: Where did Yousef practise his talk?
options: In the empty storeroom behind the gym

questions.q: What advice did Uncle Saleh give Yousef?
options: Speak to the person in the last row

questions.q: Why did the speakers suddenly go silent?
In the story, what does "applause" mean?
options: Clapping to show you liked something

questions.q: Why do you think Uncle Saleh lifted his chin when he looked at Yousef?
options: He wanted Yousef to leave the courtyard
He was angry with the boys at the back
He was reminding Yousef to look up and be brave

pages.text: Every winter, Layla's family drove from Riyadh into the desert for a weekend camping trip. This year, Grandpa Saleh came too, sitting in the back seat with his old wooden walking stick. Layla's younger brother, Omar, spent the whole journey playing games on his tablet. Layla, who was thirteen, kept checking her phone and complaining about the weak signal.

"In my day, we didn't need phones to find our way," Grandpa said with a smile. Layla tried not to roll her eyes. "Things are different now, Grandpa," she replied politely. Her father laughed and turned onto a sandy track that the map app was showing. "Don't worry, Baba," he said. "Trust the technology."

An hour later, the car suddenly made a loud noise and stopped. Father jumped out and opened the bonnet, but hot steam was pouring out of the engine. The sun was going down, and none of their phones had any signal at all. Mother tried to stay calm, but Layla could see that she was worried.

"We can't stay here all night," Father said. "The camp is too far to walk, and I have no idea which direction is closest to help." Grandpa slowly got out of the car and looked up at the darkening sky. "Wait until the stars come out," he said quietly. "Then I'll show you the way."

Soon the sky was full of stars, brighter than Layla had ever seen in the city. Grandpa pointed his stick at one small, steady star. "That is Al-Jadi, the North Star. My father taught me how to find it when I was younger than Omar." He explained that before sunset he had noticed a group of palm trees far away to the north. "Where there are palms, there is water, and where there is water, there are usually people."

Mother and Omar stayed in the car with the doors locked, while Father and Layla walked with Grandpa. Every few minutes, Grandpa stopped to check the star and change direction a little. Layla held his arm carefully on the soft sand. To pass the time, she asked him about his childhood, and he told her exciting stories she had never heard before.

After almost an hour, they saw a light shining between the palm trees. A farmer called Abu Nasser came out with a torch and welcomed them warmly with hot tea and dates. He drove his pickup truck back to fetch Mother and Omar, and the next morning he helped Father repair the car. "Your grandfather has the eyes of the old desert travellers," he told Layla with respect.

On the way home, Layla didn't touch her phone once. Instead, she asked Grandpa to teach her the names of more stars. That night, the whole family lay on a carpet on the roof of their house, looking up at the sky together. "Technology is useful," Layla said, "but some things you can only learn from family." Grandpa smiled proudly and pointed towards the North Star.

questions.q: Why couldn't the family call for help when the car stopped?
options: They had left their phones at home.

questions.q: How did Grandpa know there might be people to the north?
options: He saw a car driving north.
He had noticed palm trees there before sunset.

questions.q: In the story, what does "steady" mean when describing the star?
Who stayed in the car while the others walked?
How did Layla's feelings about Grandpa change by the end of the story?
options: She began to respect his knowledge and wanted to learn from him.
She thought he was still old-fashioned.
She was angry that he made them walk so far.

pages.text: Laila was thirteen, and she had always loved finding out how things worked. While other girls in her class collected stickers, she collected old wires, broken phones and tiny screws. Last summer, she had used a kit and some spare parts to build her own weather station. It had sensors that could measure wind speed, air pressure and the amount of dust in the air.

She fixed the station to the roof of her grandfather's farmhouse near Buraidah, among the date palms. Her cousin Hamad watched her and laughed. "Why do you need a machine for the weather?" he asked. "Just look up at the sky!" Laila ignored him and connected the station to an old tablet, so it could send her an alert if anything changed.

A week later, the whole family gathered at the farm to welcome Uncle Saad home after three years of studying abroad. The men put up a huge tent under the palm trees, and the women spread colourful rugs on the sand. The smell of rice and grilled lamb filled the air. The weather forecast on the news had promised a clear, calm evening.

In the late afternoon, Laila's tablet suddenly beeped. She checked the screen and frowned. The air pressure was dropping fast, and the dust levels were rising every minute. She had never seen numbers like these before. "Something's wrong," she told Hamad, but he only shrugged. "Your machine is probably broken," he said.

Laila didn't give up. She ran to her grandfather and showed him the screen. He read it slowly, then walked to the edge of the farm and stared at the horizon. The birds were flying low, and far away the sky was turning a strange yellow colour. "Your machine and my old eyes are telling me the same story," he said quietly. "A sandstorm is coming."

Grandfather's voice was calm but firm, and everyone listened. The family hurried to carry the food, the rugs and the youngest children into the house. Hamad helped Laila cover the generator and close every window. Only twenty minutes later, a huge brown wall of dust rolled across the fields and swallowed the palm trees.

The storm roared for almost an hour, and the wind tore the empty tent away into the darkness. Inside the majlis, however, the family sat safely on the floor and shared their dinner by lamplight. Uncle Saad told funny stories about the cold winters abroad. Hamad was unusually quiet, and at last he turned to Laila. "I'm sorry I laughed," he said. "Will you show me how your station works?"

The next morning, the sky was blue again, and everyone helped to clean the sand from the yard. Grandfather put his hand on Laila's shoulder. "Our neighbours have farms too," he said. "Could you build more of these for them?" Laila smiled and looked at Hamad, who was already holding her toolbox. "Only if I have an assistant," she said, and for the first time, Hamad didn't laugh at her idea at all.

questions.q: Why did the family gather at the farm?
What did Laila's weather station NOT measure?
In the story, 'the horizon' is…
options: the line where the sky meets the land

questions.q: Why did Grandfather believe Laila?
options: Because the TV news said a storm was coming
Because what he saw in nature matched her screen

questions.q: How had Hamad's feelings changed by the end of the story?
options: He was still jealous of Laila
He was angry about losing the tent
He respected Laila and wanted to help her

pages.text: "A hero who changed the way we see the world," Faisal read aloud from the school website. "That's easy. A footballer!" His twin brother Omar rolled his eyes. "It's a science project, Faisal, and we have to present it together on Sunday." They had been arguing for an hour when suddenly every light in the flat went out.

The living room was completely dark except for a thin line of afternoon sun. It was coming through a small hole in the old curtains. Their grandfather laughed softly from his chair. "Don't panic, boys," he said. "A thousand years ago, a great scientist sat in a dark room just like this one, and he discovered something amazing."

"His name was Ibn al-Haytham, and he lived in Cairo," Grandfather began. "The ruler there asked him to control the floods of the River Nile, but Ibn al-Haytham soon realised that the task was impossible. He was afraid of the ruler's anger, so he stayed inside his house for years. While he was there, he spent his time studying light."

"Now, look at the wall behind you," Grandfather said, pointing. The boys turned around and gasped. On the white wall, they could see a picture of the street outside. The palm tree, the minaret of the mosque, even the moving cars were all there. But everything was upside down!

"How is that possible?" Omar whispered. "Light travels in straight lines," Grandfather explained. "When it passes through a tiny hole, the lines cross over, so the picture flips. Ibn al-Haytham was the first person to explain this clearly, and later people used his ideas to build cameras."

Faisal jumped up so fast that he nearly knocked over his tea. "Omar, this is our project! We can build our own dark room and show everyone." For the next two days, the twins worked together with a cardboard box, black paper, tape and a sheet of thin white paper. Their first box didn't work because the hole was too big, but they refused to give up.

On Sunday, the classroom was full of colourful posters about famous scientists. When it was their turn, Omar closed the blinds, and Faisal invited their classmates to look inside the box one by one. "It's the school garden, and it's upside down!" shouted Hamad. Even their teacher, Mr Khalid, looked inside twice and said it was the best project he had seen all year.

That evening, the electricity was working again, but Faisal turned off the lights anyway. He watched the orange sunset slowly appear upside down on the wall. "You know," Omar said, sitting down beside him, "a hero doesn't need to score goals." Faisal smiled. "No," he agreed. "Sometimes a hero only needs a dark room and a lot of questions."

questions.q: Why did the room become dark?
options: The boys turned off the lights to sleep.

questions.q: Why did Ibn al-Haytham stay inside his house for years?
options: He was ill and could not walk.
He was afraid of the ruler's anger.
He did not like the River Nile.

questions.q: What does the word "gasped" show about the boys?
Why didn't the twins' first box work?
What has Faisal learned by the end of the story?
options: Footballers are the only real heroes.
Curiosity and asking questions can make someone a hero.

pages.text: Lina had always believed that the weather app on her phone knew everything. Her grandfather, Jiddo Saleh, believed something different. "Phones are clever," he liked to say, "but the sky has been talking for thousands of years." That Friday, the whole family drove out to a wide, dry valley for a picnic.

The sun was shining, and there wasn't a single cloud above them. Lina's little brother, Omar, was building towers of stones while their mother made tea. Lina checked the forecast: sunny, 31 degrees, light wind. "Perfect," she said, and put her phone away.

After lunch, Jiddo stood up and looked towards the mountains in the west. Dark clouds were gathering there, far away, like a grey wall. "Can you smell that?" he asked. Lina breathed in and noticed a fresh, earthy smell in the air, although the ground around her was completely dry.

"It's raining in the mountains," Jiddo said quietly. "And all that water has only one way to go: down this valley." Lina laughed nervously. "But it's sunny here! Nothing is going to happen." Just then, her phone buzzed with a warning: heavy rain and flash floods expected in the area.

Her father didn't wait. "Everyone into the cars, now!" he called. They threw the blankets and the teapot into the boot and drove up a rocky slope to the higher ground near the road. Omar complained that he hadn't finished his tower, but nobody was listening.

Ten minutes later, they heard a low roar, like a train in the distance. Then a wave of brown water rushed around the bend, carrying branches and stones. In seconds, the place where they had been sitting disappeared under a fast, muddy river. Lina held her grandfather's hand tightly and couldn't say a word.

"If we had stayed down there..." her mother began, but she didn't finish the sentence. Soon the clouds reached them too, and big, cool drops began to fall. Jiddo smiled and lifted his face to the rain. "Alhamdulillah," he said. "Rain is a blessing, as long as you respect it."

When the rain stopped, a bright rainbow appeared over the new river. Lina took out her phone, but this time she didn't check the forecast. Instead, she opened her notes and wrote: "Lesson one: listen to the phone. Lesson two: listen to Jiddo. Lesson three: never have a picnic in a dry valley when the mountains look angry." Omar read it over her shoulder and laughed, "Lesson four: build your towers higher up!"

questions.q: What was the weather like in the valley when the family arrived?

pages.text: Every morning, Faisal walked through the old streets of Al-Balad in Jeddah on his way to school. He loved the tall coral houses with their wooden windows, even though many of them were cracked and empty. One house on his street was in very bad condition, and a long crack ran across its front wall like a dark river. But on Sunday morning, Faisal stopped in surprise. Someone had painted a small blue-and-gold pattern inside the crack, like a star made of tiny triangles.

On Monday there was another star. By Tuesday, the pattern had grown into a line of shapes that followed the crack up the wall. "Who's doing this?" Faisal asked his friend Hamad as they stared at it. "Probably a famous artist," Hamad said. "Someone who wants to stay secret." Faisal took a photo with his phone, and he couldn't stop thinking about it all day.

That afternoon, Mr Nasser, their art teacher, announced the school competition. "This year the title is 'Hidden Beauty'," he explained. "I want you to find something beautiful that most people walk past without noticing." Hamad nudged Faisal and whispered, "Easy! Just show him your photos of the wall." Faisal smiled, but something felt wrong, because the art wasn't his, and he didn't even know whose it was.

So Faisal decided to solve the mystery first. On Thursday he woke up very early, prayed Fajr with his father, and asked if they could walk past the old house on the way home. The street was grey and quiet, and the air smelled of the sea. In front of the cracked wall, a boy was standing on a plastic box, holding a thin brush and a small pot of paint. When he turned round, Faisal recognised him immediately: it was Omar, the quiet new boy who sat at the back of their class.

Omar looked frightened, as if he had been caught doing something terrible. "Please don't tell anyone," he said. "This was my grandfather's house. He used to make these patterns for doors and windows, and he taught me before he died." He explained that the house had been empty for years, and every time a new crack appeared, he filled it with colour. "I didn't want it to look forgotten," he said quietly.

Faisal's father looked at the wall for a long time. "Your grandfather would be proud of you," he said finally. Then Faisal had an idea. "Omar, would you enter the art competition with me? Not with my photos of your work, but with the real story: the house, your grandfather and the patterns." Omar hesitated, then nodded slowly, and for the first time Faisal saw him smile.

For two weeks, the boys worked together after school. Omar drew the patterns his grandfather had taught him, while Faisal wrote about the history of the house and took careful photos. On the day of the exhibition, people crowded around their project, which they had called "The Wall That Woke Up". Mr Nasser read every word, and he looked surprisingly emotional. They didn't win first prize, because they came second, but something even better was about to happen.

A week later, a woman from the city heritage office visited the school, because she had seen the project and wanted to know more about the house. "We're going to repair it," she told the boys, "and we'd like you to design the patterns for the new wooden door." Omar couldn't speak at first, so Faisal answered for both of them: "We'd love to!" Now, when people walk down that street, they don't see a crack. They see a door covered in blue-and-gold stars.
